Detailed: Conventional two-dimensional radiography has limitations in detecting the true extent of periapical lesions, especially in the early stages. The dense cortical plates of bone often mask underlying changes in the less dense cancellous bone. For a periapical radiolucency to be clearly visible on a periapical radiograph, there must be sufficient destruction of bone, including the erosion of the inner cortical plate (endosteum). This means that a significant amount of bone loss may have occurred before it is radiographically apparent. Advanced imaging techniques like Cone Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) are more sensitive in detecting early or small periapical lesions because they provide three-dimensional views without the superimposition of surrounding structures.
Subject: Endodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2465): What is the most common cause of a "flare-up" during endodontic treatment?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Over-instrumentation or extrusion of debris into the periapical tissues
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Over-instrumentation or extrusion of debris into the periapical tissues
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: A flare-up is an acute exacerbation of a periapical lesion during or after endodontic treatment, characterized by pain and/or swelling. It is most commonly caused by the introduction of bacteria or irritants (like infected debris or irrigants) into the periapical tissues during instrumentation, particularly if there is over-instrumentation or apical extrusion.
Detailed: A "flare-up" refers to the development of acute pain and/or swelling in a tooth undergoing or recently completed endodontic treatment. While various factors can contribute, the most frequent cause is the disruption of the microbial balance within the root canal system and/or the mechanical, chemical, or microbial irritation of the periapical tissues. This often occurs when infected debris, bacteria, or irrigants are extruded apically during instrumentation, triggering an acute inflammatory response in the periapex. Other contributing factors can include changes in the microbial flora, inadequate debridement, or even patient stress.
Subject: Endodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2466): Which histological feature is characteristic of an acute apical abscess?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Presence of a cyst cavity lined by epithelium
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: Accumulation of lymphocytes and plasma cells
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 3: Presence of a distinct focus of neutrophils in the lesion
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Presence of a distinct focus of neutrophils in the lesion
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: An acute apical abscess is an acute inflammatory response to infection spreading from the root canal into the periapical tissues. Histologically, it is characterized by a predominance of neutrophils, indicating an active purulent infection. Chronic lesions typically show a prevalence of lymphocytes and plasma cells.
Detailed: Histological examination of periapical lesions reveals different cellular compositions depending on whether the lesion is acute or chronic. An acute apical abscess is characterized by a dense infiltration of polymorphonuclear leukocytes (neutrophils) and the formation of pus. This reflects a rapid, intense inflammatory response to bacterial invasion from the infected root canal. Chronic apical periodontitis, on the other hand, is characterized by a predominance of mononuclear cells, such as lymphocytes, plasma cells, and macrophages, which are associated with a longer-standing inflammatory process. Periapical cysts are characterized by a central lumen lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, surrounded by inflammatory connective tissue.
Subject: Endodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2467): What is the recommended management for an avulsed permanent tooth with a closed apex and a dry time exceeding 60 minutes?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Replant immediately and perform root canal treatment later
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: Replant immediately and monitor for vitality
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 3: Clean the root surface, soak in NaF, replant, and initiate root canal treatment within 7-10 days
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 4: Discard the tooth as prognosis is hopeless
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Clean the root surface, soak in NaF, replant, and initiate root canal treatment within 7-10 days
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: For avulsed teeth with a long dry time (>60 mins) and closed apex, the periodontal ligament cells are unlikely to be viable. The focus shifts to preventing resorption. Cleaning the root, soaking in NaF (to reduce root resorption), replanting, splinting, and initiating root canal treatment extraorally or soon after replantation are recommended to prevent inflammatory and replacement resorption.
Detailed: When a permanent tooth with a closed apex is avulsed and experiences a prolonged dry time (greater than 60 minutes), the prognosis for the survival of the periodontal ligament (PDL) cells is severely diminished. Replantation is still often performed to maintain the alveolar bone and aesthetic contour, but the tooth is likely to undergo root resorption. The recommended protocol involves cleaning the root surface to remove necrotic PDL tissue, soaking the root in a fluoride solution (e.g., 2% NaF for 20 minutes) to make the root surface more resistant to resorption, replanting the tooth, stabilizing it with a flexible splint, and initiating root canal treatment within 7-10 days after replantation because the pulp will become necrotic. The long-term prognosis for these teeth is guarded, with a high risk of ankylosis (replacement resorption) and inflammatory resorption.
Subject: Endodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2468): Which of the following is the most accurate statement regarding the relationship between the apical foramen and the radiographic apex in mature teeth?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: The apical foramen always coincides with the radiographic apex
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: The apical foramen is typically located 0.5-1.0 mm coronal to the radiographic apex
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 3: The apical foramen is typically located 0.5-1.0 mm apical to the radiographic apex
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 4: The location of the apical foramen is unpredictable relative to the radiographic apex
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: The apical foramen is typically located 0.5-1.0 mm coronal to the radiographic apex
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: In most mature teeth, the apical foramen, the main opening of the root canal to the periapical tissues, exits the root slightly off the anatomical and radiographic apex. It is usually located 0.5 to 1.0 mm coronal to the radiographic apex, although variations exist. Accurate working length determination considers this anatomical reality.
Detailed: The anatomical apex is the morphological tip of the root. The radiographic apex is the apex as visualized on a radiograph. The apical foramen is the actual exit point of the root canal from the root surface, which can vary in size, shape, and location. In mature teeth, the apical foramen is typically located slightly short of (coronal to) the anatomical and radiographic apex, often exiting laterally due to the deposition of cementum. An accurate working length, usually determined by an electronic apex locator and confirmed with a radiograph, should ideally terminate at the apical constriction, which is typically located coronal to the apical foramen, to ensure thorough cleaning and shaping without irritating the periapical tissues.
Subject: Endodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2469): What is the primary purpose of performing a "tug back" test when fitting a master gutta-percha cone?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: To confirm the cone reaches the full working length
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: To ensure the cone is centered in the canal
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 3: To verify adequate apical fit and resistance to displacement
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 4: To assess the flexibility of the gutta-percha cone
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: To verify adequate apical fit and resistance to displacement
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Tug back is the resistance felt when the master gutta-percha cone is seated to the full working length and then gently pulled coronally. Adequate tug back indicates that the cone fits snugly in the apical preparation, providing a good seal and suggesting that the canal has been properly shaped to receive the cone at the desired working length. Lack of tug back may indicate an undersized cone or inadequate apical preparation.
Detailed: The "tug back" test is a clinical method used during obturation to assess the fit of the master gutta-percha cone in the apical portion of the root canal preparation. When the master cone is inserted to the predetermined working length, it should ideally bind or resist withdrawal slightly within the apical 1-2 mm. This resistance, or "tug back," indicates that the apical preparation has been correctly sized and shaped and that the master cone provides a snug fit, which is important for achieving a good apical seal and preventing leakage after obturation. Insufficient tug back may require selecting a larger cone or further refining the apical preparation.
Subject: Endodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2470): Which of the following systemic conditions can mimic odontogenic pain, making accurate diagnosis challenging?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 3: Sinusitis or nerve-related conditions (e.g., Trigeminal Neuralgia)
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Sinusitis or nerve-related conditions (e.g., Trigeminal Neuralgia)
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Pain originating from non-odontogenic sources can be referred to the teeth and jaws, making it difficult to differentiate from true toothache. Maxillary sinusitis is a common cause of pain referred to posterior maxillary teeth. Neuropathic pain conditions like trigeminal neuralgia can also present as severe facial pain that patients may perceive as originating from a tooth.
Detailed: Differential diagnosis of orofacial pain is essential in endodontics. Pain perceived by the patient as originating from a tooth may, in fact, be referred pain from non-odontogenic sources. Maxillary sinusitis is a common example, where inflammation of the sinus lining can cause pressure and pain that is felt in the maxillary posterior teeth. Neuropathic pain conditions, such as trigeminal neuralgia, involve dysfunction of the trigeminal nerve and can cause intense, paroxysmal pain in the distribution of the nerve, which may be mistaken for toothache. Other non-odontogenic sources of pain include TMJ disorders, myofascial pain, and vascular pain. A thorough history, clinical examination, and appropriate diagnostic tests are necessary to differentiate between odontogenic and non-odontogenic pain.
Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2471): What is the primary goal of vital pulp therapy (e.g., pulp capping or pulpotomy) in teeth with reversible pulpitis or small pulp exposures?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: To remove the entire pulp tissue
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: To preserve the vitality and function of the remaining pulp tissue
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 3: To extract the tooth and prevent infection
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: To preserve the vitality and function of the remaining pulp tissue
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Vital pulp therapy procedures are performed in teeth with healthy or reversibly inflamed pulps that have been exposed due to caries or trauma. The objective is to protect the remaining vital pulp tissue, promote healing, and maintain its function, allowing for continued root development in immature teeth and preserving the tooth's natural defense mechanisms. This is an alternative to root canal treatment when the pulp is considered capable of healing.
Detailed: Vital pulp therapy procedures, such as direct pulp capping and pulpotomy, are aimed at maintaining the health and vitality of the dental pulp in cases of reversible pulpitis or small, clean pulp exposures. The primary goal is to protect the remaining pulp tissue from bacterial contamination and irritation, allowing it to heal and continue its physiological functions, including the formation of tertiary dentin. Preserving pulp vitality is particularly important in immature teeth to allow for continued root development. These procedures are considered when the pulp is assessed as being healthy or reversibly inflamed and free from irreversible damage or widespread bacterial infection.
Subject: Endodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(215): What is the most common reason for fixed prosthesis debonding?

When the bond fails, the prosthesis may become loose or fall off, requiring re-cementation or replacement. Ensuring proper cementation techniques and material selection is critical to the long-term success of fixed prostheses.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(339): What is the most important factor in ensuring the success of a fixed partial denture (bridge)?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(498): What is the most common cause of porcelain veneer failure?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1011): What is the primary concern when using a cantilever bridge for a posterior tooth?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1025): What is the main advantage of using zirconia for posterior crowns?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Zirconia offers exceptional strength and is highly durable, making it suitable for posterior restorations that are subject to significant occlusal forces.
Detailed: Yttria-stabilised tetragonal zirconia has a flexural strength of roughly 900 to 1200 MPa, several times greater than lithium disilicate and an order of magnitude greater than feldspathic porcelain. Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1044): What is the first step in preparing a tooth for a crown?

Depth-orientation grooves are cut to the required depth and the intervening tooth structure is then removed, following the original cuspal morphology so that the reduction is uniform.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1057): What is the main advantage of using all-ceramic crowns?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: All-ceramic crowns provide excellent esthetics, making them ideal for anterior teeth due to their ability to closely match natural tooth color.
Detailed: All-ceramic crowns transmit light in a manner closely resembling enamel and dentine, so they reproduce the depth, translucency and vitality of natural teeth in a way that a metal-supported restoration cannot. They also eliminate the grey cervical shadow and the risk of a visible metal collar as the gingiva recedes.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1058): What is the most common type of bridge used for replacing a missing tooth in the posterior region?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1060): What is the purpose of a post and core restoration in crown and bridge therapy?

Detailed: The purpose of a post and core is to provide a retentive foundation for the definitive crown when little coronal tooth structure remains. The assembly does not strengthen the root, so a ferrule of sound dentine is essential.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1077): What is the main reason for placing a post in a tooth prior to crown placement?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1094): What is the most important factor when selecting a material for a dental crown?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1137): What most commonly causes porcelain fracture in PFM crowns?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Inadequate metal support causes 80% of fractures
Detailed: Porcelain is strong in compression but weak in tension, so it fractures where the metal framework fails to support it. Sharp internal angles, abrupt changes in metal thickness, unsupported porcelain at incisal edges and connectors, and a metal-ceramic junction placed on a centric contact all concentrate tensile stress. Correct framework design with uniform 1 to 2 mm ceramic thickness is the key preventive measure.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1142): What is the most common reason for failure of a fixed dental bridge?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Improper tooth preparation can lead to bridge failure due to poor fit, retention, or lack of adequate support.
Detailed: Retention and resistance form are established by the preparation, so inadequate axial wall height, excessive taper, absence of grooves or boxes and poorly defined margins predispose a bridge to debonding, marginal leakage and subsequent caries. Because a bridge distributes load across several units, deficiencies in abutment preparation are magnified compared with a single crown.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1166): What is the main advantage of using zirconia for crown and bridge restorations?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Zirconia is known for its exceptional strength and durability, making it suitable for high-stress restorations, particularly in posterior teeth.
Detailed: Zirconia combines very high flexural strength and fracture toughness with excellent biocompatibility and low plaque affinity when polished. Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1181): Proper sequence for metal-ceramic crown try-in?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Shillingburg's try-in sequence: proximal contacts, margins, occlusion, contour, then esthetics.
Detailed: Proximal contacts are evaluated first because an over-tight contact prevents the restoration seating fully, which would invalidate any subsequent assessment of margins or occlusion. Once the crown seats, marginal integrity is verified, then occlusion in maximum intercuspation and excursions, then axial contour and embrasure form, and finally shade and surface characterisation.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1199): Why "rock" crown during cementation?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Dynamic seating ensures complete seating (Rosenstiel 2006).
Detailed: Rocking or intermittently loading the crown during cementation applies dynamic rather than static pressure, allowing the viscous cement to flow and escape from between the restoration and the preparation. This reduces hydraulic back-pressure and permits complete seating, which is essential for marginal adaptation and for keeping the cement film thickness within acceptable limits.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1237): When should shade selection be done for ceramic crowns?

Detailed: Shade is selected at the start of the appointment, before rubber dam placement or prolonged mouth opening, because teeth dehydrate rapidly once isolated and become lighter and more opaque. Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1267): A patient presents with a dark anterior crown. What property of color is being referred to?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1384): What is the most common reason for failure of a fixed bridge restoration?

Detailed: Marginal discrepancy exposes a wider band of cement to oral fluids, accelerating cement dissolution and creating a plaque-retentive step at the restoration-tooth junction. Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1447): What is the primary advantage of using all-ceramic crowns?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1466): When preparing tooth #30 for full gold crown, what is the ideal occlusal reduction?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1470): What is the most common complication following the placement of a fixed partial denture (bridge)?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1494): What is the most common complication of using a temporary crown?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1523): A 32-year-old man comes to the clinic to restore his upper first premolar with a lithium disilicate crown. The clinician prepares the tooth with excessive occlusal reduction. Which of the following is most likely to occur due to this amount of reduction?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1577): What is the best material for the retainer in a fixed partial denture (bridge)?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1601): What is the best method for restoring an endodontically treated tooth with significant tooth loss?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1610): What is the primary concern when preparing a tooth for a crown in a patient with severe bruxism?

Occlusal reduction, taper, axial wall height and additional grooves are therefore the principal preparation considerations.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1611): Which of the following is the most common reason for gingival inflammation around a ceramic crown?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1615): What is the primary disadvantage of all-ceramic crowns in the posterior region?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: All-ceramic crowns, although esthetically pleasing, lack the strength required for posterior restorations under heavy occlusal forces.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1648): When should a cantilever bridge be used in the posterior region?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1681): What is the most common material used for the coping of full porcelain crowns?

Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1683): What is the best material to use for a crown in a molar with high functional stress?

Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1709): What is the most important step in the process of creating a prosthetic crown for a patient?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Proper tooth preparation is essential for ensuring that the crown fits well and provides sufficient retention.

Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1717): What is the most common cause of tooth sensitivity after crown placement?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1755): When should a cantilever bridge be considered for use?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1759): Which of the following is an indication for using non-rigid connectors in fixed partial dentures?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1774): What is the primary purpose of the porcelain in a porcelain-fused-to-metal (PFM) crown?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1780): What is the ideal material for a crown in a patient with bruxism?

Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1786): What is the ideal preparation margin for a crown on a posterior tooth?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1792): A 45-year-old woman comes in for a routine check-up and complains of feeling that her dentures are not fitting well. Clinical examination reveals that the dentures are causing sore spots in the upper palatal area. What is the most appropriate management for this issue?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1807): What is the most important step in the process of delivering a fixed partial denture (bridge)?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1814): A 25-year-old woman presents with a complaint of discomfort in her upper central incisors, which are sensitive to cold. Clinical examination reveals a well-established crown with no visible defects. What is the most likely cause of her discomfort?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1826): What is the most common type of tooth preparation for posterior crowns?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1854): Which of the following describes the abutment position for #44 in a patient with Class 3 Mod 1 partial edentulous mandibular arch?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1949): What is the most common cause of failure in a bridge involving a cantilever abutment?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1954): What is the primary function of a bridge retainer?

Detailed: The retainer is the component cemented to the abutment tooth, and its function is to support the pontic and transmit occlusal load to the abutment while providing the retention that holds the prosthesis in place. Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1983): What is the most important consideration when preparing a tooth for a crown in a patient with a history of bruxism?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1990): What to do when crown doesn't fit abutment with large discrepancy?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1999): What is the ideal implant material for patients with a high risk of corrosion or allergic reactions?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2007): Which of the following is the most important factor when preparing abutment teeth for a fixed dental bridge?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2010): Type of porcelain fracture in chipped veneer #21?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2066): What is the most common cause of failure of a fixed partial denture (bridge)?

Detailed: Deficiencies in abutment preparation, particularly inadequate axial wall height, excessive taper, poorly defined finish lines and insufficient occlusal reduction, determine whether a bridge will retain, seal and withstand occlusal load. Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2080): What is the ideal crown to root ratio?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2091): What is the ideal margin design for a crown preparation?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2117): What is the typical thickness required for the occlusal reduction when preparing a posterior tooth for a crown?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2119): An edentulous patient presented to the clinic requesting the replacement of his upper and lower dentures. The dentures were worn for 25 years... Which definitive impression technique would be preferred?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2134): When preparing a tooth for a crown, what is the recommended taper for the walls of the preparation?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2184): What is the most common cause of failure in porcelain-fused-to-metal (PFM) crowns?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2211): How to design pontics for tissue health?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2250): A 30-year-old man comes to the clinic for a routine dental checkup. He reports mild pain in his upper left first molar when chewing. Clinical examination reveals a cracked tooth with an isolated deep carious lesion. What is the most appropriate treatment for this case?
