Detailed: Long-term reviews of conventional bridgework identify loss of retention, through debonding or cement washout and usually accompanied by caries at the retainer margin, as the leading cause of failure. This reflects the fact that the cement lute is the weakest link in a restoration subjected to repeated occlusal and thermal cycling.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4642): The term “gingival retraction” refers to:
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: Temporarily displacing gingiva to expose finish lines
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Temporarily displacing gingiva to expose finish lines
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Retraction cord or paste displaces gingiva temporarily for accurate impression.
Detailed: Gingival retraction is the temporary lateral and apical displacement of the free gingival margin to expose the finish line and a small band of unprepared tooth beyond it, so that the impression material can flow around and record the margin. It is achieved mechanically with cord, chemomechanically with impregnated cord, or surgically with electrosurgery or laser.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4644): Which impression material is most dimensionally stable for delayed pouring?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: PVS has excellent dimensional stability and can be poured multiple times.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4645): What is the purpose of using a retraction cord before impression making?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: To temporarily displace gingival tissue and expose margins
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: To temporarily displace gingival tissue and expose margins
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Retraction cords provide clear access to finish lines for impression accuracy.
Detailed: Retraction cord opens the gingival sulcus so that impression material can pass beyond the finish line, and impregnated cords simultaneously control crevicular fluid and haemorrhage. Without retraction the material cannot flow into the sulcus and the margin is either not recorded at all or is recorded as a torn, unreadable edge on the die.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4646): Which tray type is preferred for final impressions in fixed prosthodontics?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Custom trays provide better fit and minimize distortion in final impressions.
Detailed: A custom tray provides a uniform, thin layer of impression material, typically 2 to 3 mm, which reduces the total volume of material and therefore the absolute dimensional change on polymerisation. It also gives better support and control of the material and improves accuracy compared with the variable and often excessive thickness in a stock tray.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4647): What is a major disadvantage of alginate as an impression material in fixed prosthodontics?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Alginate impressions must be poured immediately to avoid distortion.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4650): Which of the following is NOT a requirement for provisional restorations?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Provisionals are temporary and don’t need to last long-term.
Detailed: Provisional restorations are required to protect the pulp, maintain the position of the prepared and adjacent teeth, preserve periodontal health, restore function and appearance, and allow evaluation of the proposed occlusion and contour. They are not required to be durable in the long term, since they are intentionally cemented weakly and are replaced within weeks.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4655): What is the working time of polyvinyl siloxane impression materials?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: PVS typically has a working time of about 3–6 minutes depending on formulation.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4656): The “double mix” impression technique involves:
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Using two different impression materials with different viscosities
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Using two different impression materials with different viscosities
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Heavy body material in tray and light body around tooth ensures accuracy.
Detailed: In the double mix or one-stage technique a heavy or putty body material is loaded into the tray while a light body material is simultaneously syringed around the prepared teeth, and the tray is seated so that both set together. This produces a homogeneous impression without a separate relief stage, at the cost of requiring two operators or careful timing.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4658): Which of these is a characteristic of polyether impression materials?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Polyether materials are very hydrophilic, making them good in moist environments.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4659): Which factor does NOT affect the setting time of impression materials?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Patient age does not influence material setting.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4660): Which temporary crown fabrication technique allows indirect fabrication outside the mouth?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Indirect technique fabricates the provisional on a model outside the mouth.
Detailed: In the indirect technique an impression or a preoperative index is used to fabricate the provisional on a cast outside the mouth, so the exothermic reaction and any unpolymerised monomer never contact the prepared tooth or the soft tissues. It generally gives better marginal fit and surface finish than the direct method, at the cost of extra time.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4662): The ideal cement thickness for permanent luting agents should be approximately:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Thin cement layers improve retention and minimize marginal gaps.
Detailed: A film thickness of approximately 20 to 40 microns permits full seating of the restoration while maintaining an intact lute. The ADA specification requires type I luting cements not to exceed 25 microns. A thicker film indicates incomplete seating, leaves an open margin exposed to dissolution, and weakens the cement layer itself.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4666): What is the main advantage of CAD/CAM technology in fixed prosthodontics?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: Increased accuracy and reduced human error
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Increased accuracy and reduced human error
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: CAD/CAM allows digital design and milling, improving precision and reducing errors in restoration fabrication.
Detailed: CAD/CAM eliminates several of the manual steps in which dimensional error accumulates, notably impression distortion, model pouring, waxing, investing and casting. Digital scanning, design and milling produce restorations with consistent and reproducible marginal accuracy, and the process is faster and permits same-day delivery.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4667): What material is commonly used for CAD/CAM milled crowns?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Zirconia is widely used for its strength, esthetics, and suitability for CAD/CAM milling.
Detailed: Zirconia is the most widely milled CAD/CAM material because it is supplied in pre-sintered blanks that mill easily and then sinter to full strength, and because its high flexural strength and toughness allow both monolithic crowns and multi-unit frameworks. Lithium disilicate and hybrid ceramics are the other principal milled materials.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4668): Which factor is critical in achieving proper occlusion in fixed prosthodontics?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Proper occlusion requires precise records of how teeth come together to avoid premature contacts or trauma.
Detailed: The definitive occlusion can only be as accurate as the records from which it was constructed. An impression that has distorted, or a bite registration that has displaced the mandible or deflected the teeth, produces mounted casts that do not represent the patient, so the restoration will require extensive chairside adjustment or will be unusable.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4671): Which occlusal scheme is recommended for fixed partial dentures to reduce stress on abutments?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: This scheme protects anterior teeth in excursions and posterior teeth in centric occlusion, reducing stress.
Detailed: In mutually protected occlusion the posterior teeth carry axial load in maximum intercuspation while the anterior teeth provide guidance that discludes them in all excursions. This protects abutment teeth from the damaging lateral forces generated by posterior interferences, which is why it is the preferred scheme for fixed prosthodontics in a dentate patient.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4673): What is a common cause of occlusal discrepancies in fixed restorations?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Poor records lead to incorrect occlusal contacts causing discomfort and failure.
Detailed: Occlusal errors in the finished restoration are most often traced to inaccurate impressions, distorted or displaced interocclusal records, or incorrect articulator mounting. Any of these means the casts do not reproduce the patient's actual relationship, so the technician constructs a technically sound restoration to the wrong occlusal scheme.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4674): Why is the die spacer applied during laboratory procedures?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: To increase the size of the die
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 3: To protect the die from damage
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Die spacer creates uniform space so cement can fit between tooth and restoration without interference.
Detailed: Die spacer creates the internal relief that the luting cement occupies. Without it the cement, which cannot escape quickly enough from a closely fitting intaglio surface, generates hydraulic pressure that holds the restoration away from the preparation. The spacer is stopped short of the margin so marginal adaptation itself remains intimate.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4675): What is the main disadvantage of porcelain-fused-to-metal (PFM) restorations?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: PFM crowns may show a dark line at the margin, compromising esthetics especially in anterior teeth.
Detailed: The opaque metal substructure and the opaquer that masks it prevent light transmission, and where the metal extends to the facial finish line a dark line is visible at the margin, becoming more conspicuous as the gingiva recedes. This aesthetic limitation is the principal reason all-ceramic systems have displaced metal-ceramic in the anterior region.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4676): Which of the following is NOT a benefit of digital impressions over conventional impressions?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Digital impression systems require significant upfront investment.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4677): What is the purpose of occlusal adjustment after cementation of a fixed prosthesis?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: Remove premature contacts and achieve harmonious occlusion
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Remove premature contacts and achieve harmonious occlusion
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Adjusting occlusion prevents trauma, discomfort, and restoration failure.
Detailed: Cementation alters the occlusal relationship slightly because the cement film raises the restoration and because the try-in was performed without the lute in place. Checking and adjusting the occlusion after the cement has set removes any resulting premature contacts, preventing periodontal ligament inflammation, sensitivity, restoration fracture and porcelain chipping.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4678): What is the minimum thickness recommended for metal coping in a PFM crown?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Metal coping thickness around 0.3 mm provides adequate strength without excessive bulk.
Detailed: A metal coping of approximately 0.3 to 0.5 mm is needed to resist distortion during porcelain firing and to support the veneering ceramic uniformly under load. Thinner copings flex, allowing the ceramic to be loaded in tension and to fracture, while excessively thick copings consume the space required for the ceramic layer.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4681): Which factor is important to prevent distortion of impression materials?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Some impression materials distort over time; pouring immediately ensures accuracy.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4684): What is the most common cause of sensitivity after crown cementation?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: Pulpal inflammation due to dentin exposure
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Pulpal inflammation due to dentin exposure
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Over-preparation or exposure of dentinal tubules can cause sensitivity post-cementation.
Detailed: Crown preparation cuts millions of dentinal tubules and the pulp is further insulted by desiccation, heat and the cementation procedure. Where the remaining dentine thickness is small, the resulting pulpal hyperaemia and hydrodynamic fluid movement in the exposed tubules produce postoperative sensitivity, which usually settles as reparative dentine forms but occasionally progresses to irreversible pulpitis.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4687): What is a common biological complication in fixed prosthodontics?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Caries can develop if margins are not well adapted or if oral hygiene is poor.
Detailed: Recurrent caries at the margin of a retainer is the classic biological complication of fixed prosthodontics. It arises where the margin is defective or subgingival, plaque control is poor, or the retainer has partially debonded without the patient noticing. Because it develops beneath a restoration it is often detected late, when the abutment is already unrestorable.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4688): Which factor most influences the esthetics of an all-ceramic crown?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Adequate ceramic thickness is essential for translucency and color matching.
Detailed: The optical behaviour of an all-ceramic crown depends primarily on how much ceramic is present to transmit and scatter light. Insufficient thickness means the underlying tooth or core shows through and the restoration appears grey and lifeless, while adequate thickness allows the layering of translucent and opaque materials that reproduces natural depth.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4691): What should be done if a fixed prosthesis fractures after cementation?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Fractured restorations must be replaced or repaired to restore function and esthetics.
Detailed: A fractured cemented prosthesis must be assessed for the cause before anything else. If the fracture is minor and the substructure intact, an intraoral repair may be acceptable as an interim measure, but a bulk fracture, a fractured framework or a repeated failure indicates that the restoration should be removed and remade after correcting the underlying cause.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4694): What is a common aesthetic complication with metal-ceramic crowns?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Metal coping can show through thin gingiva, causing a dark line at the margin.
Detailed: As the gingival margin recedes with age or following periodontal treatment, the metal collar or the opaque layer at the cervical margin of a metal-ceramic crown becomes visible as a dark line. The metal may also shadow through thin overlying mucosa. A collarless design, a porcelain butt margin or an all-ceramic restoration avoids this.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4695): Which margin type provides best esthetic results with all-ceramic crowns?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Shoulder margins provide a broad, well-defined margin needed for ceramic thickness and esthetics.
Detailed: A shoulder provides a flat platform of adequate width to support the ceramic in bulk right up to the margin, permitting a porcelain butt margin with no opaque layer visible and giving the most favourable stress distribution. This produces the best cervical aesthetics for an anterior all-ceramic restoration.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4696): What is the best way to manage gingival inflammation after crown placement?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Improve oral hygiene and remove irritants
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Improve oral hygiene and remove irritants
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Local plaque and margin irritation cause inflammation; hygiene control is key.
Detailed: Gingival inflammation after crown placement is nearly always a plaque problem created by a local irritant. Assessment should identify over-contour, a marginal discrepancy, residual subgingival cement or violation of the supracrestal attachment, and treatment consists of removing that irritant and reinforcing hygiene. Only if the tissue fails to respond is more invasive management considered.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4700): Which of the following is NOT a sign of failure in fixed prosthodontics?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Minor adjustments are normal; others indicate potential failure.
Detailed: Minor occlusal adjustment at delivery is a normal and expected part of the cementation appointment, since the cement film and the absence of the restoration during previous records inevitably alter contacts slightly. Genuine signs of failure include loss of retention, marginal discrepancy with recurrent caries, porcelain or framework fracture, persistent gingival inflammation and abutment pain.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4704): What is the primary challenge when restoring teeth with short clinical crowns?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Short clinical crowns provide less axial wall height, reducing retention and resistance. Additional procedures may be needed.
Detailed: A short clinical crown provides limited axial wall height and surface area, so both retention against removal and resistance against oblique displacement are reduced. Management options include reducing the taper as far as possible, adding grooves or boxes, using adhesive cementation, and surgically or orthodontically increasing the clinical crown height.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4705): Which procedure can increase crown height in short clinical crowns?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Crown lengthening exposes more tooth structure surgically, improving retention.
Detailed: Surgical crown lengthening removes gingiva and, where necessary, alveolar bone to expose additional coronal tooth structure, increasing the axial wall height available for retention and providing a ferrule. At least 3 mm must remain between the new bone crest and the planned margin to accommodate the supracrestal attachment and sulcus, and restoration is deferred for several weeks while the tissues stabilise.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4706): What is the ideal crown-root ratio for a tooth to serve as an abutment?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: A crown-root ratio of at least 1:2 (more root than crown) is favorable for abutment support.
Detailed: A crown-to-root ratio of 1:2 means the root within bone is twice the length of the clinical crown, which represents an ideal distribution of leverage for an abutment. In practice 2:3 is regarded as optimum and 1:1 as the minimum acceptable, since increasing the ratio lengthens the lever arm acting on progressively less periodontal support.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4710): What is the “ferrule effect” in prosthodontics?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: The use of metal posts in root canals
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: A band of tooth structure encircling the crown margin to increase fracture resistance
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: A band of tooth structure encircling the crown margin to increase fracture resistance
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Ferrule effect enhances resistance to fracture by providing bracing effect on tooth.
Detailed: The ferrule is the band of sound tooth structure encircled by the crown apical to the core, and it resists the wedging action of a post and the lateral forces applied to the crown by binding the remaining root together. A height of at least 1.5 to 2 mm with 1 mm of wall thickness is required, and its presence is the strongest predictor of survival of a post-retained restoration.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4711): Which is NOT a type of pontic design used in implant prosthodontics?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Screw-retained refers to prosthesis retention, not pontic design.
Detailed: Pontic designs are classified by their relationship to the residual ridge, and include the ovate, modified ridge lap, conical, sanitary and saddle forms. Screw retention describes how a restoration is attached to an implant abutment, not the form of the pontic itself, so it is not a pontic design.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4713): Which component connects the implant fixture to the prosthetic crown?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: The abutment is the intermediate piece connecting implant to crown.
Detailed: The abutment is the intermediate component that connects the implant fixture within the bone to the prosthetic crown above the mucosa. It is secured to the fixture by a screw and establishes the emergence profile through the soft tissue, and it may be prefabricated or custom-made, and designed for either cemented or screw-retained restorations.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4725): Which cementation protocol is recommended for all-ceramic crowns to optimize bond strength?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Acid etching of tooth and silane application on ceramic
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Acid etching of tooth and silane application on ceramic
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Proper surface treatment of both tooth and ceramic improves micromechanical and chemical bonding.
Detailed: For a glass-based all-ceramic crown, the tooth surface is etched with phosphoric acid and an adhesive applied, while the ceramic intaglio is etched with hydrofluoric acid and silanated. This provides micromechanical retention on both surfaces plus a chemical bond between silica and resin, giving the highest bond strengths and reinforcing the ceramic itself.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4727): Which type of ceramic is best suited for high strength anterior restorations?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Lithium disilicate offers excellent esthetics and good strength for anterior crowns.
Detailed: Lithium disilicate offers a flexural strength of roughly 350 to 450 MPa combined with good translucency and the ability to be etched and adhesively bonded. This combination of strength and optical quality makes it the standard choice for high-strength anterior crowns and veneers where zirconia would be too opaque and feldspathic porcelain too weak.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4728): What is the main disadvantage of zirconia restorations compared to glass ceramics?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Zirconia is strong but less translucent than glass ceramics, affecting esthetics.
Detailed: Zirconia is a dense polycrystalline material that scatters light strongly rather than transmitting it, so conventional 3Y-TZP appears opaque and lifeless compared with glass ceramics. Newer 4Y and 5Y translucent grades improve this but at the cost of significantly reduced flexural strength, so a trade-off between appearance and strength is unavoidable.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4730): Which occlusal factor increases risk of crown fracture?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Lateral forces cause tensile stresses that can fracture brittle restorations.
Detailed: Lateral excursive contacts apply force at an angle to the long axis of the tooth, generating tensile and shear stresses in a material that is strong only in compression. Interferences on a ceramic restoration during working or non-working movements are therefore a major cause of chipping and bulk fracture, and their elimination is an essential part of delivery.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4731): What is the effect of increasing cement film thickness on crown retention?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Thick cement layers reduce friction and fit, lowering retention.
Detailed: An increased cement film thickness indicates that the restoration has not seated completely, which reduces the frictional contact between the intaglio surface and the preparation and leaves a wider band of cement exposed at the margin. Both effects reduce retention, and the exposed lute is then progressively dissolved by oral fluids.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4737): What is the primary reason for occlusal wear on opposing teeth caused by zirconia crowns?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Zirconia is very hard and can cause wear if surface is not properly polished or glazed.
Detailed: Zirconia has very high hardness, and when its surface is left rough after adjustment it acts as an abrasive against the opposing enamel. Well-polished zirconia is in fact kinder to opposing teeth than glazed feldspathic porcelain, so any adjustment must be followed by systematic repolishing with diamond-impregnated polishers rather than reglazing alone.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4740): What is the effect of contamination with saliva during cementation?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: Reduced bond strength and marginal seal
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Reduced bond strength and marginal seal
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Saliva interferes with bonding agents reducing adhesion and increasing microleakage.
Detailed: Saliva contamination of an etched or primed surface deposits glycoproteins that block the microporosities and prevent resin infiltration, dramatically reducing bond strength and leaving a defective marginal seal. If contamination occurs the surface must be cleaned and re-etched or re-primed according to the manufacturer's protocol before cementation proceeds.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4741): Which method improves seating of crowns during cementation?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Applying pressure helps fully seat the crown and reduce excess cement.
Detailed: Applying sustained finger or biting pressure, ideally with intermittent dynamic loading, allows the viscous cement to flow and escape from the interface so the restoration can seat completely. Adequate venting through the cement escape channels created by die spacer, and avoidance of an over-filled intaglio surface, are equally important.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4742): What is the purpose of “try-in” pastes in cementation?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: To check fit and shade before final cementation
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: To check fit and shade before final cementation
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Try-in pastes simulate the optical and seating properties of final cement.
Detailed: Try-in pastes are water-soluble glycerine-based analogues of the definitive resin cement, supplied in matching shades. They allow the clinician and patient to evaluate the seated appearance and the final shade with the restoration in place before irreversible cementation, and they are simply rinsed away before the definitive cement is applied.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4747): Which is the best technique to ensure proper marginal adaptation of a provisional crown?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: Using a matrix or putty index from diagnostic wax-up
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Using a matrix or putty index from diagnostic wax-up
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Matrices guide precise fabrication and ensure accurate margins and contour.
Detailed: An index or matrix formed from a diagnostic wax-up or from the preoperative tooth contour reproduces the intended external form exactly, so the provisional requires minimal adjustment and its margins can be finished accurately against the preparation. This gives better marginal adaptation, contour and occlusion than free-hand fabrication.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4749): What is the recommended method for disinfection of impressions before sending to the lab?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: Immerse in appropriate disinfectant for recommended time
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Immerse in appropriate disinfectant for recommended time
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Proper disinfection prevents cross-contamination while preserving impression accuracy.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4754): Which factor is important for patient comfort during impression procedures?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Using warm water to mix materials
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: Selecting appropriate tray size and ensuring adequate room in mouth
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Selecting appropriate tray size and ensuring adequate room in mouth
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Proper tray fit prevents gagging and discomfort during impressions.
Detailed: Comfort during impression taking depends substantially on tray selection: a tray that is too large impinges on the soft tissues and provokes gagging, while one that is too small gives inadequate material thickness and poor extension. An appropriately sized tray with adequate clearance, seated slowly with the patient upright and breathing through the nose, greatly improves tolerance.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4757): Which protocol helps reduce gag reflex during impression taking?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Use smaller tray, distraction techniques, and quick setting materials
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 3: Ask patient to breathe through the nose only
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Use smaller tray, distraction techniques, and quick setting materials
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: These methods reduce discomfort and improve patient tolerance.
Subject: Removable Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4761): Which is the best method to communicate shade selection to the laboratory?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Using a shade guide with digital photographs and written notes
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Using a shade guide with digital photographs and written notes
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Detailed communication ensures accurate shade matching in the final restoration.
Detailed: Shade communication is most reliable when several methods are combined. A shade tab held adjacent to the tooth and photographed with the same lighting gives the technician both a reference standard and the tooth's actual appearance, while a written prescription and a shade map describing distribution of hue, chroma, translucency and characterisation complete the information.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4762): What is the ideal appointment sequence for fixed prosthodontic treatment?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: This sequence allows proper planning, tooth preparation, temporization, and final restoration placement.
Detailed: Fixed prosthodontic treatment follows a logical sequence: diagnosis and treatment planning with study casts and any wax-up, tooth preparation, impression and shade selection, fabrication and fitting of the provisional, and finally try-in and cementation of the definitive restoration. Each stage depends on the completion of the previous one.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4763): How should impression materials be stored before pouring?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: In a sealed plastic bag with a damp paper towel to maintain humidity
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: In a sealed plastic bag with a damp paper towel to maintain humidity
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Maintaining humidity prevents distortion, especially with hydrocolloid materials like alginate.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4764): A 45-year-old patient presents with a missing mandibular first molar. Adjacent second molar has a large amalgam restoration, and the mandibular second premolar has healthy tooth structure. Which is the best abutment selection for a fixed partial denture?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Use only the second molar as abutment (cantilever bridge)
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: Use only the second premolar as abutment
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 3: Use both second premolar and second molar as abutments
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 4: Avoid FPD and recommend implant only
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Use both second premolar and second molar as abutments
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Using two abutments distributes occlusal load better, increasing longevity and reducing risk of failure.
Detailed: With a large existing restoration in the second molar and a sound second premolar, using both teeth as abutments distributes the load across two roots and provides adequate periodontal support for the pontic. The second molar requires full coverage in any case because of its existing restoration, so the additional biological cost of using it as an abutment is small.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4765): During tooth preparation for a metal-ceramic crown, the patient reports persistent sensitivity after cementation despite proper technique. What is the most likely cause?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Excessive axial reduction leading to dentin exposure
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Excessive axial reduction leading to dentin exposure
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Over-preparation can irritate the pulp causing sensitivity post-cementation.
Detailed: Persistent sensitivity after a technically correct cementation most often reflects over-reduction of the axial walls, which cuts a greater number of dentinal tubules and reduces the remaining dentine thickness protecting the pulp. The result is pulpal hyperaemia and hydrodynamic sensitivity that may take weeks to settle or may progress to irreversible pulpitis.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4766): You notice a fixed partial denture debonded from an abutment tooth 2 weeks after cementation. What is the most likely cause?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Poor tooth preparation and lack of retention form
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Poor tooth preparation and lack of retention form
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Insufficient taper, short axial walls, or inadequate surface area leads to poor retention.
Detailed: Early debonding within weeks of cementation almost always indicates that the preparation did not provide adequate retention and resistance form, most often through excessive taper, insufficient axial wall height or absence of grooves and boxes. Cement selection can compensate to a degree but cannot substitute for deficient preparation geometry.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4767): A patient has an anterior all-ceramic crown with a noticeable dark margin at the gingival third. What is the probable cause?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: An ALL-CERAMIC crown has no metal coping. A dark cervical margin comes from insufficient reduction leaving ceramic too thin to mask the substrate.
Detailed: A dark cervical band on an all-ceramic crown indicates that the ceramic is too thin at the margin to mask the underlying tooth or core, which occurs when the shoulder has not been prepared to adequate width. Correction requires either a wider shoulder at a repreparation or, if the substrate is discoloured, an opaque core material.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4768): A provisional crown fractured during chewing on a posterior tooth. What should you do next?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Remake or repair provisional restoration to protect the tooth
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: Wait until the final crown is ready
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 4: Use stronger cement on existing provisional
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Remake or repair provisional restoration to protect the tooth
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Protecting the prepared tooth from sensitivity and contamination is essential.
Detailed: A fractured provisional leaves the prepared dentine exposed to bacterial and thermal insult and allows the prepared and adjacent teeth to move, which will compromise the fit of the definitive restoration. The provisional must therefore be repaired or remade immediately, and the cause investigated, since fracture usually indicates inadequate thickness or a premature occlusal contact.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4769): A patient reports difficulty cleaning around the pontic area of a fixed partial denture, leading to gingival inflammation. What pontic design is likely used?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Saddle pontics cover the entire edentulous ridge, making hygiene difficult and causing inflammation.
Detailed: The saddle or ridge lap pontic overlaps the ridge broadly on both buccal and lingual aspects, creating a concave tissue surface that cannot be reached with floss or a brush. Plaque accumulates in this area and produces chronic inflammation of the underlying mucosa, which is why the design is regarded as obsolete and is replaced by modified ridge lap or ovate forms.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4770): While trying in a zirconia crown, you notice poor marginal fit despite good occlusion. What laboratory step most likely caused this?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Inaccurate scanning or milling during CAD/CAM fabrication
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Inaccurate scanning or milling during CAD/CAM fabrication
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Digital errors in scanning or milling can cause marginal gaps.
Detailed: When occlusion and proximal contacts are correct but the margin does not adapt, the error lies in the digital reproduction of the finish line. Common causes are an incompletely captured or blurred margin in the intraoral or laboratory scan, incorrect margin marking in the design software, or milling burr wear producing loss of fine detail.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4772): A patient with a short clinical crown requires a crown. You decide to perform crown lengthening. What biological structure must be respected to avoid chronic inflammation?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Respecting biologic width avoids violation of epithelial and connective tissue attachments to prevent inflammation.
Subject: Periodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4773): You observe marginal leakage on a cast gold crown after several years. What is the most probable cause?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Marginal gaps often result from long-term cement breakdown.
Detailed: Marginal leakage developing after several years of service in a cast restoration indicates progressive dissolution or washout of the cement lute at the margin, particularly with soluble cements such as zinc phosphate or glass ionomer. As the lute is lost, a gap forms which retains plaque and permits recurrent caries at the margin.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4775): You are fabricating a provisional crown for a molar tooth. Which technique offers best marginal fit and occlusal accuracy?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Using a matrix from diagnostic wax-up and direct chairside fabrication
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 4: Using only autopolymerizing resin without matrix
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Using a matrix from diagnostic wax-up and direct chairside fabrication
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Matrix guides accurate shape and margin formation for better fit.
Detailed: Using a matrix taken from a diagnostic wax-up or from the preoperative anatomy reproduces the intended contour precisely, so the provisional requires minimal adjustment, while direct chairside fabrication allows the margins to be relined and finished against the actual preparation. This combination gives the best combination of marginal fit and occlusal accuracy.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4776): A patient with a resin-bonded bridge shows recurrent caries on abutment tooth. What preventive step could have been missed?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Proper oral hygiene instruction and plaque control
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Proper oral hygiene instruction and plaque control
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Plaque accumulation due to poor hygiene around abutments can cause caries.
Detailed: Resin-bonded bridges have extensive enamel coverage with a wing that creates a plaque-retentive margin, so recurrent caries reflects inadequate plaque control at that margin. Preventive management therefore requires specific hygiene instruction covering the wing margins and beneath the pontic, together with fluoride and dietary advice and regular review.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4778): A patient’s all-ceramic crown fractures 1 year after placement. The crown had minimal occlusal clearance. What likely caused the fracture?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Insufficient occlusal reduction leading to thin ceramic thickness
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Insufficient occlusal reduction leading to thin ceramic thickness
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Thin ceramic areas are prone to fracture under functional loads.
Detailed: Insufficient occlusal reduction leaves the ceramic too thin, and the flexural stress generated in a thin section under occlusal load concentrates at the intaglio surface where microcracks propagate to failure. Verifying clearance with a reduction guide or a putty index before the impression prevents this, since no laboratory technique can compensate for inadequate space.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4781): A patient’s tooth preparation shows undercuts in axial walls. What is the best correction method?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Remove undercuts using rotary instruments before impression
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: Use a more flexible impression material
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Remove undercuts using rotary instruments before impression
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Eliminating undercuts prevents impression distortion and poor restoration fit.
Detailed: Undercuts prevent the restoration from seating along a single path of insertion, and they cannot be blocked out on the die without leaving a corresponding void at the tooth surface. They must therefore be eliminated at the preparation stage with rotary instruments before the impression is recorded, and the preparation checked from the occlusal direction with a single line of sight.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4782): During cementation, you notice that the crown does not seat fully due to interference. What should you do?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Identify and adjust the interfering area before recementing
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: Apply more cement and force seating
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 3: Remove cement and try again without adjustment
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 4: Send crown back to lab without adjustment
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Identify and adjust the interfering area before recementing
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Adjusting interferences ensures complete seating and prevents stress on restoration or tooth.
Detailed: Incomplete seating from an internal interference must be diagnosed and corrected before any attempt at definitive cementation, because cementing an unseated restoration produces an open margin and a thick lute. Fit-checking material or disclosing spray identifies the point of premature contact, which is then relieved on the intaglio surface until the restoration seats passively.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4783): A patient complains of a “metal taste” after cementation of a PFM crown. What is the most likely cause?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Corrosion of metal alloy and exposure of metal margins
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Corrosion of metal alloy and exposure of metal margins
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Metal exposure and corrosion can cause metallic taste and tissue irritation.
Detailed: A metallic taste after cementation of a metal-ceramic crown suggests galvanic activity or corrosion, occurring where base metal alloy is exposed at the margin or where the restoration contacts a dissimilar metal restoration through saliva acting as an electrolyte. It is more common with base metal alloys than with high-noble alloys.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4785): During impression making, you notice bleeding around the prepared tooth. What is the best management?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Use hemostatic agents and retraction cord before taking impression
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Use hemostatic agents and retraction cord before taking impression
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Controlling bleeding improves impression accuracy and margin clarity.
Detailed: Blood and crevicular fluid prevent the impression material from wetting and adapting to the finish line, producing voids and drags at the margin. Haemostasis must therefore be achieved before the impression is taken, using retraction cord impregnated with aluminium chloride or ferric sulphate, or a haemostatic paste, with adequate time allowed for the tissue to stop bleeding.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4786): A patient with a history of bruxism has recurrent fractures of all-ceramic crowns. What prosthetic modification can improve longevity?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Use zirconia cores with adequate thickness
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Use zirconia cores with adequate thickness
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Zirconia is stronger and more resistant to fractures in high-stress patients.
Detailed: In a bruxist the restoration must survive sustained heavy and eccentric loading. A high-strength zirconia core of adequate thickness, or a fully monolithic zirconia restoration with no veneering layer to chip, provides the necessary fracture resistance. This should be combined with occlusal adjustment to eliminate interferences and a protective occlusal splint.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4787): You observe poor esthetics in a maxillary anterior crown due to a greyish hue. What is the likely cause?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Dark underlying tooth structure or metal coping
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Dark underlying tooth structure or metal coping
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Underlying substrate color affects final shade, especially with thin ceramics.
Detailed: A greyish appearance in an anterior crown results from insufficient light transmission, which occurs either because a metal coping or opaque core blocks light or because the underlying tooth is discoloured and the ceramic is too thin to mask it. Correction requires adequate reduction, an opaque core or internal characterisation, or lightening the substrate.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4788): A patient complains of food impaction under a fixed partial denture pontic. What design modification can help?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Use an ovate pontic to contour tissue
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: Use a sanitary pontic with no tissue contact
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Use an ovate pontic to contour tissue
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Ovate pontics sit slightly into the tissue, improving food deflection and esthetics.
Detailed: An ovate pontic has a convex tissue surface that is received into a concavity in the ridge, producing an intimate seal with the mucosa and eliminating the space in which food collects. It requires adequate ridge volume, achieved by socket preservation at extraction or by soft tissue augmentation, and demands careful cleaning with superfloss.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4789): You have a patient with a deep subgingival margin making impression difficult. What technique can help?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Electrosurgery or laser gingival retraction to expose margins
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Electrosurgery or laser gingival retraction to expose margins
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Temporarily displacing tissue allows clear access for accurate impressions.
Detailed: Where the finish line lies deep within the sulcus and cord alone cannot expose it, tissue can be removed surgically with electrosurgery or a soft tissue laser to uncover the margin and simultaneously achieve haemostasis. Care is required to respect the supracrestal attachment, since removing tissue too close to the bone crest provokes recession and inflammation.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4790): After cementation, a patient develops sensitivity and swelling in the gingival area adjacent to a crown margin. What is the most likely cause?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Excess cement can irritate soft tissues causing inflammation and discomfort.
Detailed: Cement extruded into the sulcus and not removed acts as a foreign body and a plaque-retentive surface, producing localised inflammation, swelling and sensitivity. Meticulous removal of excess cement, verified with an explorer, floss and where necessary a radiograph, is essential, and the risk is one of the main arguments in favour of screw-retained implant restorations.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4792): A patient with limited mouth opening requires fixed prosthodontic treatment. What impression technique can help?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Use a sectional or split impression tray
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Use a sectional or split impression tray
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Sectional trays allow impression in parts, overcoming restricted opening.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4793): You notice localized inflammation around an abutment tooth after bridge placement. What should you evaluate first?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Poor margins and plaque accumulation cause inflammation.
Detailed: Localised inflammation at an abutment after bridge placement should first prompt assessment of the restoration margin and the patient's ability to clean it. Marginal discrepancy, over-contour, residual cement and violation of the supracrestal attachment are all local irritants that can be identified by probing, radiography and inspection, and correcting them resolves most cases.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4795): A patient complains of persistent bad taste after cementation of a crown. What is a common cause?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Cement left subgingivally can cause irritation and taste disturbance.
Detailed: A persistent unpleasant taste after cementation is most often caused by residual excess cement retained in the sulcus or in an embrasure, where it accumulates plaque and undergoes bacterial degradation. Careful inspection with an explorer and floss, supplemented by a radiograph for proximal areas, identifies and allows removal of the remnant.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4796): You observe a fixed prosthesis with an open margin visible on radiograph but no clinical symptoms. What is the recommended action?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: If no symptoms exist, close monitoring and hygiene can prevent progression.
Detailed: An asymptomatic open margin visible only on radiograph, with no caries, sensitivity or gingival inflammation, does not automatically require replacement, since remaking a restoration carries its own biological cost. The site is monitored radiographically at review, hygiene is reinforced and topical fluoride applied, and intervention is undertaken if caries or symptoms develop.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4800): A patient with heavy occlusal forces requires a fixed prosthesis. What material choice would you recommend?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Zirconia core with PFM or monolithic zirconia crown
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Zirconia core with PFM or monolithic zirconia crown
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: High strength materials resist fracture under heavy load better.
Detailed: For a patient generating heavy occlusal loads, the restoration must have both high flexural strength and resistance to chipping. A monolithic zirconia crown or a zirconia core with carefully supported veneering ceramic provides this, eliminating or minimising the weak veneering layer that delaminates under parafunctional load.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4801): You observe marginal discoloration around a crown in a patient with poor oral hygiene. What is the likely cause?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Marginal gaps allow bacterial infiltration leading to discoloration and caries.
Detailed: Marginal discolouration in a patient with poor hygiene indicates plaque accumulation at a marginal discrepancy, with staining of the exposed cement lute and early microleakage. It should be regarded as a warning sign of developing recurrent caries and managed with hygiene reinforcement, fluoride and close radiographic review.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4802): During cementation, you observe that the crown seats with difficulty. What is the recommended protocol?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Remove interferences by adjusting restoration or tooth
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Remove interferences by adjusting restoration or tooth
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Proper seating prevents stress on tooth and restoration and ensures fit.
Detailed: When a restoration will not seat, the interference must be located and eliminated rather than forced. Fit-checking material or disclosing spray applied to the intaglio surface reveals the premature contact, which may be a nodule on the internal surface, an over-tight proximal contact or a residual undercut on the tooth, and the appropriate surface is then adjusted.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4810): The “rest” in an RPD serves primarily to:
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: Transfer occlusal forces to the abutment tooth
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Transfer occlusal forces to the abutment tooth
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Rests transmit occlusal loads to the abutment, preventing tissue impingement.
Detailed: The rest is the component that transmits vertical occlusal load to the abutment tooth along its long axis, providing the vertical support that prevents the prosthesis settling into the underlying mucosa. By maintaining the framework in its planned position it also preserves the relationship of the clasp arms to the survey line and prevents impingement on the gingival tissues.
Subject: Removable Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4819): Which impression technique is most appropriate for distal extension RPDs?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Functional impressions capture soft tissue under functional load, improving fit.
Detailed: A distal extension base is supported partly by teeth, which move about 0.1 mm, and partly by mucosa, which is displaceable by up to 2 mm. A functional or mucodisplacive impression records the edentulous ridge in a loaded state so that the base is supported in the position it will occupy during function, which equalises support and reduces rotation and torque on the abutments.
Subject: Removable Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4839): What impression material is preferred for final impressions of the edentulous areas in distal extension RPDs?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: These materials provide good accuracy and dimensional stability for mucosal tissues.
Detailed: Polyether and addition silicone are both elastomers with high accuracy, good elastic recovery and excellent dimensional stability, which is essential when the impression must record both rigid abutment teeth and displaceable mucosa in one procedure. Polyether has the advantage of hydrophilicity and rigidity, while addition silicone has superior long-term dimensional stability.
Subject: Removable Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4840): What is the primary purpose of border molding in RPD impressions?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: To record functional extension of denture borders for retention and stability
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: Improve impression accuracy of teeth only
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: To record functional extension of denture borders for retention and stability
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Border molding shapes the peripheral seal, enhancing retention.
Detailed: Border moulding records the depth and width of the functional sulcus by having the patient perform the muscle movements that will occur in service. This produces a denture border that is maximally extended without impinging on moving tissue, which is the basis of the peripheral seal and therefore of retention, and it also prevents displacement of the prosthesis during function.
Subject: Removable Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4850): Which impression technique improves soft tissue capture in distal extension cases?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Functional border molding and wash impression
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 4: Use of rigid impression trays only
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Functional border molding and wash impression
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: This captures tissue in function, improving fit and comfort.
Detailed: In a distal extension case the tissues distal to the last abutment are mobile and their functional form differs markedly from their resting form. Border moulding the custom tray followed by a light-body wash records these tissues in the position they occupy under load, giving a base that is intimately adapted during function rather than only at rest.
Subject: Removable Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4858): What is the role of tissue stops in impression trays for RPDs?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Provide stable seating and prevent distortion
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Provide stable seating and prevent distortion
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Tissue stops maintain consistent thickness of impression material.
Detailed: Tissue stops are small projections of tray material contacting the ridge at defined points. They prevent the tray from being seated too deeply into the impression material, maintain a uniform space for the material, and stabilise the tray while the impression sets, all of which reduce distortion and give a more accurate and reproducible result.
Subject: Removable Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4869): During clinical examination, an abutment tooth exhibits mobility. What is the impact on RPD design?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: May contraindicate use of the tooth as abutment or require splinting
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: May contraindicate use of the tooth as abutment or require splinting
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Mobile teeth may not withstand forces; stabilization or exclusion is necessary.
Detailed: A mobile abutment has reduced periodontal support and cannot resist the additional loading imposed by clasps and rests. Design options include splinting the tooth to adjacent teeth to distribute the load, selecting a more flexible clasp such as wrought wire, redistributing support to other teeth, or in severe cases excluding it as an abutment altogether.
Subject: Removable Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4871): What is the role of the proximal plate on an abutment tooth?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Contact guiding planes and resist lateral displacement
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Contact guiding planes and resist lateral displacement
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Proximal plates stabilize the denture by engaging guiding planes.
Detailed: The proximal plate contacts the prepared guiding plane on the abutment, providing bracing against horizontal displacement, defining a single path of insertion and contributing frictional retention. In the RPI assembly it also disengages from the guiding plane as the framework rotates under functional load, releasing stress from the abutment.
Subject: Removable Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4878): What impression technique best captures the functional form of movable mucosa in distal extension areas?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Captures tissue under function, improving denture fit and comfort.
Detailed: Mobile mucosa over a distal extension area assumes a different form under load than at rest. A functional impression, in which the border is moulded by muscle activity and the tissues are recorded under controlled pressure, captures this functional form so that the denture base remains adapted while the patient is chewing rather than only when the mouth is at rest.
Subject: Removable Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4890): Which impression technique provides the most accurate cast for an RPD framework?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Dual impression technique using custom tray and functional border molding
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Dual impression technique using custom tray and functional border molding
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: This captures detailed tooth and tissue anatomy for precise fabrication.
Detailed: The dual or altered cast technique records the abutment teeth with a conventional accurate impression for the framework, and then records the edentulous extension areas separately under functional load with a custom tray attached to the fitted framework. This produces a cast in which the tooth-supported and tissue-supported components are related to each other as they will be in function.
Subject: Removable Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4905): During impression taking, the patient gags easily. What technique can reduce gag reflex?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Use sectional impression trays or digital impression
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Use sectional impression trays or digital impression
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Reducing tray size and using newer techniques minimize gagging.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4909): What is the main reason for fabricating a custom tray for RPD impressions?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Improve impression accuracy by controlling material thickness and border molding
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Improve impression accuracy by controlling material thickness and border molding
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Custom trays allow precise impression technique for better fit.
Detailed: A custom tray provides a uniform, thin and controlled space for the impression material, usually 2 to 3 mm, which minimises the absolute dimensional change on setting and improves accuracy. Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(12): What is the most common technique-related cause of early failure in resin composite restorations?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Moisture contamination during placement can compromise the bonding strength of the composite restoration.
Detailed: Poor isolation during the placement of resin composite restorations is a very common cause of failure. Moisture contamination from saliva, blood, or crevicular fluid can significantly compromise the bonding process between the composite material and the tooth structure. Resin composites rely on a meticulous bonding technique that involves etching the enamel and dentin, applying a bonding agent, and then placing the composite in layers and light-curing each layer. Moisture interferes with the effectiveness of the etching and bonding agents, leading to a weaker bond strength. This weakened bond can result in microleakage (seepage of fluids and bacteria at the restoration-tooth interface), postoperative sensitivity, recurrent caries, and ultimately, the failure of the restoration. While inadequate curing also leads to failure by not fully polymerizing the resin, and poor technique can contribute, moisture control through proper isolation using a rubber dam or other effective methods is paramount for the long-term success of composite restorations.
Subject: Operative

Detailed: The retention of amalgam restorations primarily depends on mechanical locks. This means that the restoration is physically retained in place due to the roughness of the cavity walls and the shape of the prepared tooth. According to Black's principles of cavity preparation, specific angles (90° cavosurface angles) and minimal convergence are essential to ensure that the restoration is held firmly in place. The cavity preparation is designed so that the amalgam can interlock with the tooth structure, minimizing movement and dislodgement.
Subject: Operative

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(317): What is the main advantage of resin-modified glass ionomer over traditional glass ionomer?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Resin-modified glass ionomer offers improved bond strength to enamel and dentin compared to traditional glass ionomer.
Detailed: 315: The main advantage of resin-modified glass ionomer (RMGI) over traditional glass ionomer (GI) is its significantly improved bond strength to tooth structure (enamel and dentin). RMGIs incorporate hydrophilic resin monomers and a photoinitiator, allowing them to cure via a dual-cure mechanism (acid-base reaction of GI plus light-activated polymerization of the resin). Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(8): What is the most common cause of a retained root in the maxilla?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Retained roots are often the result of incomplete extraction, where portions of the tooth root remain embedded in the bone or soft tissue.
Detailed: The most common cause of a retained root in the maxilla is an incomplete extraction. This occurs when a portion of the tooth root breaks off and remains embedded in the alveolar bone or surrounding soft tissues during the tooth removal process. Several factors can contribute to root fracture during extraction, including brittle or curved roots, ankylosis (fusion of the tooth root to the bone), or the application of excessive or improper force during the procedure. While root fracture can lead to a retained root, the primary reason for its presence is the failure to completely remove all root fragments at the time of extraction. Infection or anatomical variations might complicate extractions and potentially increase the risk of root fracture, but the direct cause of a retained root is the incomplete removal of the tooth structure.
Subject: Oral Surgery

Detailed: A Hawley retainer is often the preferred choice for retaining a tooth that has been corrected from a crossbite. Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(209): Which of the following is the most important factor when planning treatment with a functional appliance for a patient?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Skeletal age is the primary factor for determining the appropriate timing of treatment.
Detailed: (207) Skeletal age is the most important factor when planning treatment with a functional appliance for a patient. Functional appliances are designed to correct skeletal malocclusions, and their effectiveness largely depends on the patient's developmental stage. Skeletal age, which reflects the maturity of the skeletal system, determines the optimal timing for intervention. The goal of using functional appliances, such as a Herbst appliance or Twin-Block, is to modify the growth of the jaws to correct discrepancies in the bite. If applied too early, the treatment may be ineffective, as the skeletal structures may not be receptive to the changes. Conversely, if applied too late, the potential for growth may be limited. By assessing skeletal age, orthodontists can determine when a patient is in the optimal phase for this kind of treatment.
Subject: Orthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(216): In Angle’s classification, when the mesiobuccal cusp of the maxillary first molar is mesial to the buccal groove of the mandibular first molar, what class is it?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: A mesial position of the MB cusp defines a Class II molar relationship.
Detailed: (214) A Class II molar relationship is characterized by the mesiobuccal cusp of the maxillary first molar being positioned mesial to the buccal groove of the mandibular first molar. This indicates a malocclusion where the upper teeth are positioned too far forward relative to the lower teeth. In Angle's classification of occlusion, a Class II relationship is commonly associated with a retruded mandible or an overjet, where the upper teeth protrude beyond the lower teeth. This condition may require orthodontic intervention to correct the skeletal discrepancy and improve the occlusal relationship. The Class II molar relationship is commonly treated with functional appliances or fixed orthodontic braces.
Subject: Orthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(224): What is the main benefit of using functional appliances in orthodontics?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Functional appliances are designed to correct skeletal discrepancies by influencing jaw growth.
Detailed: (222) The main benefit of using functional appliances in orthodontics is to correct skeletal discrepancies, particularly in patients with malocclusion. These appliances work by stimulating growth in the jawbones, which helps in correcting issues like overbites or underbites. Functional appliances such as the Herbst appliance or the Twin-Block appliance are commonly used in growing patients to guide the growth of the mandible and maxilla. These devices are effective in improving the alignment of the teeth and jaws without the need for extractions or surgery. By modifying the jaw growth in a controlled manner, functional appliances improve both the functional and esthetic outcomes of orthodontic treatment. They are most effective during periods of active skeletal growth, making early intervention key for optimal results.
Subject: Orthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(229): Which of the following is the most common method for treating a narrow maxillary arch?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: A palatal expander is the most effective method for expanding the upper jaw in patients with a narrow maxillary arch.
Detailed: (227) The most common method for treating a narrow maxillary arch is the use of a palatal expander. A palatal expander is an orthodontic appliance designed to widen the upper jaw by gradually separating the two halves of the palate. This is particularly effective in children and adolescents who are still in the growth phase, as their palatal sutures are not yet fully fused. The expansion helps to create more space for the teeth and corrects issues such as crossbite and crowding. Palatal expanders work by applying gentle pressure to the bones of the upper jaw, causing them to gradually separate, thus widening the arch. The appliance is typically used for several months and can significantly improve the alignment of the teeth and overall occlusion.
Subject: Orthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(245): In the management of a mandibular fracture, what is the most important consideration in ensuring proper healing?

Detailed: (243) Adequate fixation is the most important consideration in ensuring proper healing of a mandibular fracture. When a patient suffers a mandibular fracture, the two broken pieces must be properly aligned and stabilized to promote healing. Adequate fixation can be achieved through the use of plates, screws, or wires that hold the fragments together. This alignment ensures that the bone heals in the correct position, preventing complications such as malocclusion or further injury. Pain management and nutrition are also important, but they are secondary to proper fixation in the healing process.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(3): A 40-year-old presents with a slowly growing swelling of the posterior mandible. Radiographs show a multilocular "soap-bubble" radiolucency with internal septations and marked buccolingual cortical expansion. Which diagnosis is most consistent with these findings?

Detailed: 1. Ameloblastoma is a benign odontogenic tumor most commonly affecting the mandible.2. Radiographically, it presents as a multilocular radiolucency with internal septations, giving a soap-bubble appearance.3. Cortical expansion and thinning are hallmarks of this lesion.4. Central giant cell granuloma can also present multilocular but often in younger patients and with more heterogeneous septal patterns.5. Odontogenic keratocysts may be uni- or multilocular but typically lack significant expansion.6. Myxomas produce a tennis-racket septation pattern and occur in a younger age group.7. The lesion in this image demonstrates both pronounced cortical expansion and coarse septa.8. The location in the posterior mandible further supports ameloblastoma.9. Radiographic boundaries are well-defined and corticated.10. Soap-bubble appearance is highly suggestive of ameloblastoma.11. Differential diagnosis should still include keratocyst and myxoma but clinical correlation is essential.12. Histopathologic examination confirms diagnosis.13. Treatment requires surgical resection with clear margins.14. Recurrence rates are high without adequate margins.15. Early detection through radiographs facilitates appropriate referral.
Subject: Pathology

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4): A radiograph shows a well-defined radiolucent lesion at the apex of a non-vital tooth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: The periapical granuloma is the most common periapical radiolucency; a radicular cyst cannot be distinguished from it radiographically and is less frequent. Definitive distinction requires histology.
Detailed: A periapical cyst is the most likely diagnosis for a well-defined radiolucent lesion located at the apex of a non-vital tooth. Radiographically, it typically appears as a dark (radiolucent) area with smooth, corticated (well-defined) borders surrounding the root apex. This type of lesion is a common sequelae of pulp necrosis, where bacterial invasion and inflammation of the dental pulp lead to the formation of a cyst. The cyst is lined by epithelium and filled with fluid. While a periapical granuloma is also a radiolucent lesion at the apex, it usually presents with less defined borders. A periapical abscess may show similar radiolucency but often indicates a more acute and aggressive infection, potentially with less distinct margins. Condensing osteitis, conversely, is a radiopaque lesion indicating bone sclerosis in response to chronic low-grade inflammation.
Subject: Pathology

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(5): A multilocular radiolucent lesion in the right mandibular ramus shows scalloped margins extending between the roots and striking mesiodistal growth with minimal buccolingual expansion. What is the most likely diagnosis?

It is benign but locally aggressive with high recurrence, so enucleation is combined with peripheral ostectomy or Carnoy solution.
Detailed: The radiographic description of a multilocular radiolucent lesion in the right mandibular ramus, often described as having a "soap bubble" or "honeycomb" appearance, is highly characteristic of a Keratocystic Odontogenic Tumor (KCOT). KCOTs are benign but locally aggressive developmental cysts that originate from remnants of the dental lamina. Their multilocular appearance, with multiple cystic compartments, is a key radiographic feature that helps differentiate them from other lesions. Ameloblastomas can also be multilocular but may have a more varied radiographic presentation. Dentigerous cysts are typically unilocular and associated with the crown of an impacted tooth. Aneurysmal bone cysts, while radiolucent, often exhibit a more expansile and sometimes "blow-out" appearance, and are less commonly described with the classic "soap bubble" pattern of a KCOT.
Subject: Pathology

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(222): A 40-year-old woman has multiple mixed radiolucent-radiopaque periapical lesions confined to the mandibular anterior region; all associated teeth respond normally to vitality testing. What is the most probable diagnosis?

There are three stages in its development: the radiolucent stage, the mixed stage, and the radiopaque stage. While it is generally a benign lesion, in rare cases, it may develop complications such as infection or may be confused with more aggressive lesions like osteosarcoma. The management of cement-osseous dysplasia is typically conservative, with regular monitoring and radiographic follow-ups.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(223): What is the most common cause of oral cancer?

Detailed: (221) Smoking and alcohol use are the most significant risk factors for the development of oral squamous cell carcinoma, one of the most common forms of oral cancer. Smoking leads to the accumulation of carcinogens in the oral cavity, and alcohol consumption can act as a solvent, enhancing the absorption of these carcinogens. The combination of smoking and alcohol use significantly increases the risk of oral cancer, particularly in the tongue, floor of the mouth, and oropharynx. Human papillomavirus (HPV) has also been recognized as a contributing factor, particularly in oropharyngeal cancers, but smoking and alcohol remain the primary risk factors. Early detection through regular oral examinations and avoiding these risk factors can significantly reduce the risk of oral cancer.
Subject: Pathology

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(241): Which condition appears as bilateral white striations on buccal mucosa?

The striae are typically asymptomatic, though the condition may cause burning sensations, especially when consuming spicy or acidic foods. Nitrous oxide, when inhaled in appropriate concentrations mixed with oxygen, produces a state of conscious sedation. Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(9): A 30-year-old woman presents with localized gingival recession and root exposure on the maxillary canine and premolar. She desires aesthetic improvement. Which of the following treatment options is most appropriate for managing this case?

Detailed: Gingival grafting is the most appropriate treatment option for managing localized gingival recession with root exposure, especially when the patient's primary concern is aesthetic improvement. Gingival recession involves the apical migration of the gingival margin, exposing the root surface, which can lead to sensitivity and an undesirable appearance. Gingival grafting procedures aim to restore the lost keratinized tissue by surgically transferring a graft of gingival tissue from a donor site (often the palate) to the recipient site. This not only covers the exposed root, reducing sensitivity and the risk of further recession, but also improves the overall aesthetics by creating a more harmonious gingival architecture. Crown lengthening surgery involves removing bone and gingival tissue to expose more of the tooth's crown, which is not indicated for recession. Orthodontic extrusion can bring the tooth and the attached gingiva coronally, but it's a more extensive treatment and not solely for recession. Desensitizing agents address sensitivity but do not correct the recession or improve aesthetics.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(185): A 48-year-old man suffers from stage 3 grade B periodontitis. Medical history reveals diabetes. A sub-antimicrobial dose of doxycycline is suggested as an adjunct to mechanical therapy. Which of the following is the most suitable dose?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(218): A 40-year-old man presented to the clinic with persistent bad breath, a metallic taste in the mouth, and occasional bleeding during brushing. Detailed: (216) The radiopaque band-like pattern observed along the roots of the mandibular anterior teeth is most likely due to the presence of calculus. Subject: Periodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(225): Function of index finger in non-working hand during scaling

Detailed: (223) The function of the index finger in the non-working hand during scaling is lip retraction. The index finger is used to gently retract the lip or cheek, keeping the area clear and allowing the dental hygienist or dentist to perform the scaling procedure more effectively. By pulling back the soft tissue, the clinician ensures better access to the teeth and gums, reduces the risk of injury to the soft tissues, and improves the precision of cleaning and scaling around the tooth surface. Proper retraction also helps in maintaining patient comfort by preventing the lips from interfering with the procedure.
Subject: Periodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(228): A 32-year-old man complains of changes in the gum line around tooth #44. The clinical exam reveals gingival recession with obvious clefting. Most likely cause?

Detailed: (226) Gingival recession with obvious clefting around tooth #44 is most likely caused by improper use of dental floss. When dental floss is used incorrectly, especially if it is snapped into the gums or if excessive force is applied, it can cause trauma to the gingival tissues, leading to recession. The trauma can also result in the formation of clefts in the gum line, making the tissue more prone to further recession. Proper flossing techniques, such as gently sliding the floss between the teeth and curving it around each tooth to remove plaque, can prevent such injuries. If gingival recession occurs, it may require professional treatment, including root planing, and in some cases, gingival grafting to restore the lost tissue.
Subject: Periodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(231): A patient with periodontal disease has developed significant gingival recession and exposed roots. Which of the following procedures is most appropriate for improving the aesthetics and function of the patient's gums?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Gingival grafting can help cover exposed roots and improve the appearance and function of the gums.
Detailed: (229) Gingival grafting is the most appropriate procedure for improving the aesthetics and function of gums in patients with significant gingival recession and exposed roots. Gingival grafting involves taking tissue from another part of the mouth, such as the palate, and transplanting it to the affected area to cover the exposed roots. This procedure not only restores the aesthetics of the gums but also protects the roots from further damage and sensitivity. Gingival grafting is commonly used for cases where the gum recession is causing functional problems, such as difficulty brushing or food retention in the exposed areas. It is especially beneficial for patients with thin gingival biotypes or those who are experiencing progressive recession.
Subject: Periodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(244): What is the best method to preserve an avulsed tooth?

Storing the tooth in milk helps to maintain the cells’ vitality for several hours, allowing for a better chance of successful reimplantation. If milk is not available, a saline solution or the patient’s own saliva can also be used, but milk is the preferred option due to its optimal balance of nutrients.
