Subject: Oral Surgery

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1716): What is the main reason for using a partial-thickness (split-thickness) flap in mucogingival surgery?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: A partial-thickness flap leaves the periosteum on bone, providing a vascular bed for grafts or for apical repositioning of the flap - procedures whose goal is to increase the width of attached (keratinized) gingiva.
Subject: Periodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1862): A 32-year-old woman presents to the clinic for surgical removal of a maxillary first molar tooth. Medical history reveals 2nd trimester pregnancy. During extraction, she starts to feel drowsy and she faints. Which of the following is the first step in management for this case?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 3: Putting the patient in supine position
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 4: Putting the patient on her left side
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Putting the patient on her left side
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: A pregnant patient in the second or third trimester who faints must be placed on her LEFT side (or supine with the right hip elevated to displace the uterus leftwards). The supine position is the cause of the problem: the gravid uterus compresses the inferior vena cava, reducing venous return - supine hypotensive syndrome.
Subject: Oral Surgery

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2078): A 27-year-old man presented with inflamed operculum over partially impacted mandibular left third molar. After acute phase management, which will be the appropriate treatment?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: A partially impacted mandibular third molar that has caused pericoronitis is definitively treated by extraction of the tooth once the acute infection has been controlled. Operculectomy is followed by recurrence in most impacted teeth because the underlying lack of eruption space persists.
Subject: Oral Surgery

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2480): In Le Fort II fracture with CSF rhinorrhea, first management is:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Traumatic CSF rhinorrhea accompanying a Le Fort II fracture is initially managed conservatively: head elevation, avoidance of nose blowing, and prophylactic antibiotics to guard against ascending meningitis while the fracture is reduced. Most leaks seal spontaneously or after fracture reduction; endoscopic dural repair is reserved for leaks persisting beyond 7-10 days.
Detailed: Most traumatic CSF leaks close spontaneously within days, especially once the fracture is reduced and fixed. First-line care is therefore conservative (bed rest, head elevation, stool softeners, no nose blowing) with antibiotic prophylaxis per local protocol. Persistent leaks are localized with imaging and closed endoscopically.
Subject: Oral Surgery

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2498): In the FDI two-digit tooth numbering system, the number 36 designates which tooth?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: In FDI notation the first digit names the quadrant (3 = permanent lower left) and the second the tooth position from the midline (6 = first molar), so 36 is the permanent lower left first molar.
Detailed: Quadrants 1-4 cover the permanent dentition (upper right, upper left, lower left, lower right) and 5-8 the primary dentition in the same order. The primary lower left second molar, for example, is 75.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2635): To minimize maxillary sinus entry when removing deep maxillary third molars, the preferred approach is:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Maxillary third molars, including deeply placed ones, are removed through the standard buccal approach with a buccal mucoperiosteal flap and careful distobuccal bone removal. A palatal approach endangers the greater palatine vessels and offers no access advantage; care is taken to support the tuberosity and avoid displacing the tooth into the sinus.
Detailed: The buccal approach with a buccal mucoperiosteal flap is the standard for maxillary third molars at any depth: distal bone is removed judiciously and the tuberosity protected. A palatal approach endangers the greater palatine vessels and offers no protection against sinus entry.
Subject: Oral Surgery

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2643): During sagittal split osteotomy, the branch most at risk from lateral retraction is the:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: It runs on lateral aspect of ramus near osteotomy site.
Detailed: Excessive lateral soft-tissue retraction can stretch the buccal nerve, causing transient paresthesia.
Subject: Oral Surgery

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2650): To assess free-flap vascular patency post-reconstruction, the gold standard is:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Clinical examination - flap color, capillary refill, turgor, temperature and pinprick bleeding - remains the gold standard for monitoring free-flap perfusion, supplemented by handheld Doppler. CT angiography is reserved for equivocal cases and is not a routine monitoring tool.
Detailed: Clinical observation - flap color, capillary refill, turgor, temperature and pinprick bleeding - remains the gold standard of free-flap monitoring, supplemented by Doppler assessment. CT angiography is reserved for equivocal findings, not routine surveillance.
Subject: Oral Surgery

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2756): A patient complains that their implant-supported crown feels loose. What is the most likely cause?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: High occlusal loads can cause loosening or failure of the implant-supported crown.
Detailed: Managing occlusion helps prevent implant instability and the loosening of the restoration.
Subject: Oral Surgery

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2802): Ellis Class III fracture of a primary maxillary incisor in a 4-year-old is best managed by:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: A complicated (Ellis III) crown fracture of a primary incisor in a 4-year-old - a tooth still years from exfoliation - is treated by partial (Cvek-type) pulpotomy over the exposure with a calcium hydroxide or calcium silicate dressing, preserving the vital tooth (IADT guidelines). Extraction is reserved for unrestorable teeth or those near exfoliation.
Detailed: Partial (Cvek-type) pulpotomy preserves the vital radicular pulp of a primary incisor still years from exfoliation, maintaining the tooth for esthetics, function and space. Extraction is reserved for non-restorable teeth or infection threatening the permanent successor (IADT primary-teeth guideline).
Subject: Oral Surgery

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2927): In a 6-year-old with deep bite and palatal impaction of maxillary incisors, treatment should begin by:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Expansion creates space for incisor eruption.
Detailed: Rapid maxillary expansion opens the arch and alleviates impaction risk of permanent incisors.
Subject: Orthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(3581): A 16-year-old with palatally impacted lower canine and complete root formation. Next step?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Saves tooth and alveolar bone
Detailed: Surgical exposure via closed flap and bonding of traction attachment allows guided eruption of the impacted canine into the arch, preserving bone and function.
Subject: Orthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4067): In virtual implant planning, which CBCT-derived dataset is essential?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Segmentation data define bone and soft-tissue volumes for guide design.
Detailed: DICOM SEG objects store segmented regions (e.g., mandibular canal, bone) extracted from CBCT, critical for accurate implant guide fabrication and surgical planning.
Subject: Radiology

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(143): What is the term for the condition where the upper teeth protrude beyond the lower teeth?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: The horizontal distance by which the upper incisors protrude beyond the lower incisors is the overjet. Overbite is the VERTICAL overlap of the incisors - the two terms are frequently confused.
Detailed: Overjet is the HORIZONTAL distance between the labial surface of the lower incisors and the incisal edge of the upper incisors (normal 2-3 mm). Overbite is the VERTICAL overlap of the incisors. Increased overjet characterizes Class II division 1 malocclusion and raises trauma risk to the prominent upper incisors.
Subject: Orthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(148): What is the most appropriate treatment for a patient with anterior open bite?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Anterior open bite of skeletal origin in a growing patient is managed by controlling vertical growth - high-pull headgear or posterior bite blocks intrude/restrain the molars, allowing the bite to close by mandibular autorotation. Arch expansion addresses transverse, not vertical, discrepancies.
Detailed: Open-bite management depends on etiology and age: habit cessation for digit sucking, vertical control (high-pull headgear, bite blocks, TAD-supported molar intrusion) in growing skeletal cases, and orthognathic surgery (Le Fort I posterior impaction) for severe adult skeletal open bites.
Subject: Orthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(211): A 13-year-old with Class II skeletal malocclusion due to a retruded mandible needs mandibular growth enhancement. Which appliance is useful?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Functional appliances stimulate mandibular growth to improve Class II malocclusion.
Detailed: (209) A functional appliance is used to enhance mandibular growth in patients with Class II skeletal malocclusion due to a retruded mandible. These appliances work by applying forces to the jaw that stimulate the growth of the mandible. The goal is to correct the skeletal discrepancy by encouraging forward growth of the lower jaw while preventing the upper jaw from growing further. Functional appliances like the Herbst appliance or Twin-Block are commonly used for this purpose. These devices are typically most effective during periods of active skeletal growth, making them ideal for younger patients. The application of these appliances results in better facial aesthetics and occlusion without the need for surgical intervention.
Subject: Orthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(489): A patient complains of a bad taste after getting a 3-unit fixed partial denture. Bubbles appear on the retainer upon occlusal pressure. What is the most likely cause?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: Loosening of the retainer on the abutment
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 3: Connector fracture adjacent to the retainer
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 4: Accumulation of food debris beneath the pontic
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Marginal failure leads to leakage, causing a bad taste and bubbles under pressure.
Detailed: 487: A bad taste after a fixed partial denture with bubbles on the retainer upon occlusal pressure is most likely due to Open margins of the retainer allowing microleakage and bacterial activity.
Subject: Fixed Prosthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(570): Which material property is most critical for orthodontic brackets?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: High modulus (stiffness) prevents deformation during archwire activation
Detailed: 568: Stiffness (High modulus) is a critical material property for orthodontic brackets, allowing them to resist deformation when the archwire is activated, effectively transferring forces to the teeth.
Subject: Orthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(944): Which factor most affects orthodontic tooth movement?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Optimal 50-100g for tipping
Detailed: 942: Force magnitude is the factor that most significantly affects the rate and type of orthodontic tooth movement, with optimal force ranges required for efficient and safe tooth movement.
Subject: Orthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1064): What is the most common complication of orthodontic treatment?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Enamel demineralization around brackets - white-spot lesions progressing to decay - is the most common complication of fixed orthodontics, affecting up to half of patients with poor hygiene. Clinically significant root resorption is much less frequent.
Subject: Orthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1068): What is the main concern when placing orthodontic bands around molars?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: The main concern with orthodontic bands is demineralization and caries: bands retain plaque, and cement washout under a loose band leaves enamel bathed in cariogenic biofilm, producing decalcification (white spot lesions) and interproximal caries. Meticulous hygiene and fluoride are essential.
Subject: Orthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1338): What is the most appropriate appliance for a patient with severe anterior crossbite?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Functional appliances can help reposition the lower jaw or upper teeth to correct anterior crossbite.
Subject: Orthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1567): What is the most common complication in orthodontic treatment?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Root resorption is a common complication that can occur during orthodontic treatment, especially with excessive force.
Subject: Orthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(3544): A 12-year-old with 7 mm mandibular crowding and Class I molars. Least invasive resolution?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Conserves arch length in mild–moderate crowding
Detailed: Interproximal reduction of incisors creates up to 4 mm space while maintaining arch form and avoiding extractions.
Subject: Orthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(3617): A 17-year-old with transverse deficiency and nasal obstruction. Combined RPE should:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Addresses airway and skeletal widening together
Detailed: Combining RPE with septoplasty improves nasal airflow and maxillary expansion outcomes, optimizing both functional and orthodontic results.
Subject: Orthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(3618): A 12-year-old with moderate crowding and thin alveolar housing needs maxillary expansion. Which method is most appropriate?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Skeletal expansion with RME opens the midpalatal suture, which is still patent at 12, gaining width without tipping teeth through thin buccal bone.
Detailed: Dentoalveolar expanders (quad-helix, Schwarz plate) and bracket-based "expansion" move teeth buccally by tipping, risking dehiscence and recession through thin alveolar housing. SARPE is reserved for skeletally mature patients. Orthopedic RME is therefore the most appropriate choice in a growing 12-year-old.
Subject: Orthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(3632): A 17-year-old complains of bracket “burn” sensation. Cause?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Overetching causes sensitivity
Detailed: Prolonged enamel etching creates deeper microporosities, leading to postoperative sensitivity (“etch-burn”) when brackets are bonded; reduce etching time to 15 s.
Subject: Orthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(3851): In Roth prescription, the canine bracket tip value is:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Roth canine brackets incorporate 7° of tip for proper angulation.
Detailed: Roth prescription defines tip (second-order) values; a 7° tip built into canine brackets ensures ideal arch coordination.
Subject: Orthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(3862): After corticotomy-assisted orthodontics, the regional acceleratory phenomenon (RAP) typically subsides after approximately how many months?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: The regional acceleratory phenomenon peaks at about 1-2 months after corticotomy and then declines, subsiding to baseline by approximately 4 months - which defines the window for accelerated tooth movement.
Detailed: RAP begins within days of surgery, peaks at 1–2 months, and returns to baseline by 4–6 months, defining the optimal window for accelerated tooth movement.
Subject: Orthodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(74): What is the primary indication for performing a submandibular sialadenectomy?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: A sialadenectomy is indicated for benign tumors or persistent infections of the submandibular gland that do not respond to other treatments.
Detailed: (72): A sialadenectomy is indicated for benign tumors or persistent infections of the submandibular gland that do not respond to other treatments. The procedure involves the removal of the affected gland or tumor to prevent recurrent infection or further complications.
Subject: Oral Surgery

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(171): A patient presents with painless, firm swelling of the gingiva around a newly erupted tooth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: A firm, painless gingival swelling is a fibroma (focal fibrous hyperplasia) - the most common benign soft tissue mass, produced by chronic low-grade irritation. A pyogenic granuloma is soft, red-purple and bleeds readily; a gingival abscess is painful and fluctuant.
Detailed: Oral fibromas are collagenous reactive hyperplasias, most common on the buccal mucosa and gingiva. Treatment is conservative excision plus removal of the irritant; recurrence is rare. Histology shows dense collagen under thinned epithelium.
Subject: Periodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(239): A 3-year-old child presents with a small bump on the gums near the upper incisors. The lesion is soft and movable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: A soft, movable (often bluish) bump on the alveolar ridge of a young child overlying an erupting tooth is an eruption cyst - a dentigerous cyst variant in soft tissue. The attached gingiva contains no minor salivary glands, so a true mucocele cannot arise there.
Detailed: Eruption cysts usually rupture spontaneously as the tooth breaks through and need no treatment; simple incision of the roof is reserved for symptomatic or long-persisting lesions. Blood-filled variants ("eruption hematoma") look purple-blue and are equally innocent.
Subject: Pedodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(258): A 35-year-old male presents with swelling in the anterior floor of the mouth and difficulty swallowing. The swelling is firm and non-tender, and the patient reports that the symptoms have been present for several months. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Sialolithiasis is the most common cause of non-tender swelling in the floor of the mouth, often leading to difficulty swallowing.
Detailed: (256) Sialolithiasis is the most likely diagnosis for a patient presenting with swelling in the anterior floor of the mouth and difficulty swallowing. This condition is characterized by the formation of a salivary stone (sialolith) in one of the major salivary glands, most commonly the submandibular gland. The swelling is usually firm and non-tender, and the patient may experience difficulty swallowing due to blockage of the duct. Treatment typically involves removal of the stone through sialendoscopy or surgery.
Subject: Oral Surgery

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(321): A 45-year-old man presents with a painful swelling on the roof of the mouth. Upon examination, there is a dome-shaped swelling that is compressible and fluctuant. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: A mucocele is a fluid-filled swelling caused by the rupture of a salivary gland duct, often found on the soft palate or lower lip.
Detailed: 319: A painful, compressible, and fluctuant dome-shaped swelling on the roof of the mouth (palate) in a 45-year-old man is most likely a Mucocele. While mucoceles are most commonly found on the lower lip, they can occur anywhere minor salivary glands are present, including the palate. A mucocele results from trauma or blockage to a minor salivary gland duct, causing mucus to spill into the surrounding connective tissue, forming a pseudocyst. The swelling is typically soft, compressible, and may fluctuate in size. A ranula is a similar lesion but occurs specifically in the floor of the mouth, usually associated with the sublingual gland.
Subject: Pathology

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(344): A 30-year-old male presents with a painful lesion in the mandibular anterior region. Radiographs show a radiolucency around the roots of the mandibular incisors. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: A painful lesion with a radiolucency around the root apices indicates acute inflammatory periapical pathology of pulpal origin - a periapical abscess. Developmental odontogenic cysts are typically painless unless secondarily infected.
Detailed: 342: A painful lesion in the mandibular anterior region with a radiolucency around the roots of the incisors in a 30-year-old male is most likely a Periapical abscess or cyst originating from pulpal necrosis. Pain and a radiolucency associated with the root apex (periapical area) are classic signs of pulpal pathology, usually caused by deep caries, trauma, or cracks leading to infection and inflammation in the pulp and surrounding bone. An odontogenic cyst is a broad category; while some cysts occur in this region, a painful, acute presentation around the root apices is most often indicative of inflammatory periapical pathology (abscess or cyst secondary to infection), not a developmental cyst like a dentigerous cyst (around the crown) or an OKC (which can be in the mandible but may have a different radiographic appearance and less acute pain unless infected).
Subject: Endodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(491): A 40-year-old male presents with severe pain and swelling in the right mandible. Radiographs show a well-defined, unilocular radiolucency around the mandibular first molar. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Severe pain and swelling with a well-defined unilocular radiolucency around the roots of a first molar indicate inflammatory periapical pathology - a periapical (radicular) cyst or abscess arising from a necrotic pulp. An odontogenic keratocyst is usually asymptomatic and grows anteroposteriorly with little expansion.
Detailed: 489: A well-defined, unilocular radiolucency around a mandibular first molar with severe pain and swelling is most likely a Periapical cyst or abscess, indicating infection of pulpal origin, rather than an asymptomatic OKC.
Subject: Endodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(724): Which of the following findings identifies an incipient carious lesion?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1016): When to biopsy a painless white cheek lesion that hasn’t changed in size?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1082): A 45-year-old male presents with a swelling on the lower lip that has fluctuated in size over several weeks. The lesion is soft, dome-shaped and bluish, and he recalls repeatedly biting his lip. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: A mucocele is a benign swelling caused by the accumulation of mucus in a blocked salivary duct, commonly seen on the lower lip.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1120): What is the first step in managing a patient with oral squamous cell carcinoma?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: The first step in managing oral squamous cell carcinoma is excision and biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and determine the appropriate treatment.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1138): A 25-year-old female presents with an asymptomatic swelling in the upper jaw. On examination, the lesion is firm, mobile, and located between the central incisors. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: A firm, MOBILE, asymptomatic swelling is a soft tissue lesion - a fibroma (focal fibrous hyperplasia). A central giant cell granuloma is a central (intrabony) lesion and therefore cannot be mobile.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1376): A 30-year-old woman presents with a soft, compressible, painless swelling in the floor of the mouth that has been present for 2 weeks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Ranulas are mucous retention cysts that appear as soft, painless swellings, often near the floor of the mouth.
Subject: Oral Surgery

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1444): A 50-year-old male presents with a painless, firm, slowly enlarging lump at the junction of the hard and soft palate that has been present for several months. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Slow-growing, painless masses in the jaw are often benign salivary gland tumors, which can be treated with surgical excision.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1582): A 48-year-old patient presents with a well-circumscribed radiolucency surrounding the crown of an unerupted, impacted tooth #13, attached at the cementoenamel junction. The lesion is asymptomatic. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: A dentigerous cyst is a common developmental cyst that surrounds the crown of an unerupted tooth, often discovered incidentally.
Subject: Pathology

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1669): A 50-year-old patient presents with a swelling on the anterior portion of the jaw, which is soft, painless, and movable.
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: A soft, painless, freely movable swelling - often with a yellowish hue and a positive "slip sign" - is classic for lipoma. Fibromas are firm on palpation.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(1945): A 60-year-old male with a history of tobacco use presents with a painless lump on the floor of his mouth. Radiographs show a radiolucent lesion around the roots of the mandibular incisors. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: A persistent painless lump in the floor of the mouth of a 60-year-old tobacco user - a high-risk site and a high-risk patient - must be regarded as oral squamous cell carcinoma until biopsy proves otherwise; associated bone radiolucency suggests invasion. Ranulas occur in young patients and are soft, translucent-bluish swellings.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2192): A patient presents with an ulcer on the lateral border of the tongue that has persisted for 6 weeks despite removal of a sharp adjacent cusp. The ulcer has indurated, rolled borders. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Persistent, non-healing ulcers on the lateral border of the tongue in adults are often indicative of oral squamous cell carcinoma.
Subject: Pathology

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2233): A 28-year-old patient presents for evaluation of tooth #4, which is non-vital. Radiographs show a well-defined radiolucency at the apex, with no signs of acute infection. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: An asymptomatic well-defined apical radiolucency on a non-vital tooth represents chronic apical periodontitis; histologically it may be a granuloma or a radicular cyst, and radiographs cannot reliably distinguish the two.
Detailed: A well-defined periapical radiolucency in an asymptomatic tooth with no signs of infection represents chronic apical periodontitis, which histologically may be a granuloma or a radicular cyst. Radiographic features cannot reliably distinguish the two. Both are initially managed by orthograde root canal treatment, and only lesions that fail to heal on review are considered for surgical exploration and histopathology.
Subject: Endodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2242): What is the most appropriate first step in diagnosing a patient with a painful, swollen submandibular gland?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: For a painful, swollen submandibular gland the first diagnostic step is ultrasound: it detects stones, ductal dilatation and abscess formation non-invasively. Sialography is contraindicated in acute sialadenitis because injected contrast can push infection deeper into the gland.
Subject: Oral Surgery

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2243): A 28-year-old woman presents with white patches on the tongue and oral mucosa. The patches are not removable with a cotton swab, and the patient reports a history of burning sensation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Bilateral white patches of the tongue and buccal mucosa that cannot be wiped off, accompanied by a burning sensation in a young woman, are characteristic of oral lichen planus (reticular/erosive). Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2914): The pH of 38% SDF solution is approximately:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2931): The recommended curettage depth for a marsupialized dentigerous cyst is:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Only opening and suturing is required; curettage unnecessary initially.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2935): Which oral lesion in children is associated with iron (ferrous) supplement ingestion?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Iron compounds precipitate on filiform papillae.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4459): A 25-year-old presents with painful white plaques on lateral tongue that cannot be scraped off, biopsy shows epithelial hyperplasia without dysplasia. Diagnosis?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: A white plaque that cannot be scraped off, showing hyperkeratosis and epithelial hyperplasia without dysplasia on biopsy, is leukoplakia - a clinical diagnosis of exclusion requiring follow-up. Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(318): A 7-year-old child presents with dark staining on the upper molars. The stains are not removable with cleaning. What is the most likely cause?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(23): Which is the FIRST histologic stage of gingivitis, appearing 2-4 days after plaque accumulation?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: The initial lesion appears 2-4 days after plaque accumulation and is dominated by vasculitis and neutrophil migration. It is followed by the early lesion (lymphocytes, 4-7 days), the established lesion (plasma cells) and, if progression occurs, the advanced lesion (periodontitis).
Detailed: Gingivitis is a condition that progresses through several stages. Stage 1, the Initial stage, occurs 2-4 days after plaque accumulation, characterized by neutrophil infiltration. Stage 2, Early gingivitis, is marked by redness, swelling, and the presence of immune cells. Stage 3, Established gingivitis, involves chronic inflammation, and Stage 4, Advanced gingivitis, also known as periodontitis, results in significant tissue damage, including bone loss and tooth mobility. Early intervention is crucial to prevent progression to periodontitis.
Subject: Periodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(83): A 36-year-old man is complaining of pain while chewing related to an upper left premolar. Clinical examination revealed normal probing depths around all of his teeth, except for a 7 mm pocket in the distobuccal area of tooth #25. Detailed: A solitary deep, narrow probing defect with an isolated vertical radiolucency in an otherwise periodontally healthy mouth - with pain on chewing - is the classic presentation of vertical root fracture, especially in root-filled or heavily restored teeth. Periodontitis produces generalized or multi-site attachment loss, not a single narrow defect. Confirmation may need surgical exploration or CBCT; management of a true VRF in a single-rooted tooth is extraction.
Subject: Periodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(4150): Which immune cell type is primarily responsible for tissue destruction in periodontitis?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Macrophages release enzymes and cytokines that contribute to tissue breakdown.
Detailed: Macrophages act as key regulators in periodontal inflammation by secreting various mediators that amplify immune responses. Their persistent activation sustains chronic inflammation, resulting in progressive tissue degradation. They also interact with T and B lymphocytes, influencing the adaptive immune response. Targeting macrophage activation pathways has been explored as a therapeutic approach to limit tissue destruction in periodontitis. Macrophages infiltrate periodontal tissues in response to bacterial challenge, producing pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β, TNF-α, and prostaglandins that drive the inflammatory cascade. These mediators stimulate matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), enzymes that degrade collagen and extracellular matrix, leading to connective tissue destruction. Additionally, macrophages promote osteoclast differentiation, contributing to alveolar bone resorption. While neutrophils act early to phagocytose bacteria, macrophages orchestrate prolonged inflammation and tissue damage characteristic of periodontitis.
Subject: Periodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(17): Rubber dam wrinkling between isolated maxillary anterior teeth despite correctly spaced punch holes. Cause?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(126): Which of the following is contraindicated in patients with sickle cell disease?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(518): An 8-year-old growing patient presents with a skeletal Class II malocclusion and deep bite. What appliance would you recommend?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(2856): The critical pH for enamel demineralization is:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6001): Which irrigant/conditioner is used to remove the smear layer because it chelates the inorganic (mineral) component?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6002): Which cavity design has the highest configuration factor (C-factor) and therefore the greatest polymerization shrinkage stress?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6003): What is the primary purpose of placing composite resin in increments of 2 mm or less?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6004): Glass ionomer cement adheres to tooth structure primarily by:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6005): In selective caries removal of a deep lesion close to the pulp, dentin over the pulpal floor is excavated to which endpoint?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6006): A thin white line appearing along the margin of a composite restoration immediately after finishing most likely represents:

Subject: Operative

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6007): The main biologic function of a calcium hydroxide liner in a deep cavity is to:

Subject: Operative

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6008): Cusp coverage (capping) during restoration of a posterior tooth is indicated when:

Detailed: Onlay or cusp-capping designs replace weakened cusps with restorative material, distributing occlusal load and preventing catastrophic cuspal fracture, especially in endodontically treated posterior teeth.
Subject: Operative

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6009): Which matrix technique gives the most predictable tight proximal contact in a Class II composite restoration?

Detailed: Circumferential bands tend to flatten the proximal contour and leave light contacts with composite, which does not condense like amalgam; the sectional system compensates by pre-wedging and ring separation.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6010): The most common cause of failure of pit-and-fissure sealants is:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6011): The principal advantage of sodium hypochlorite over other endodontic irrigants is its ability to:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6012): The ideal apical termination of root canal preparation and obturation is:
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 4: At the apical constriction, about 0.5-1 mm short of the radiographic apex

Subject: Endodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6013): A mandibular central incisor most commonly requires special attention during access because it may contain:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6014): In MTA apexification of a necrotic immature tooth, the recommended thickness of the apical MTA plug is approximately:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6015): Immediately after a sodium hypochlorite extrusion accident, the FIRST step is to:

Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Recognition, patient information, saline lavage and pain control are the immediate priorities, followed by cold compresses then warm compresses and review.
Detailed: Severe swelling, ecchymosis and pain characterize the accident. Analgesics, antibiotics when indicated, and close follow-up are required; most cases resolve, but tissue necrosis and paresthesia can occur.
Subject: Endodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6016): Which feature of the pain response to cold best indicates IRREVERSIBLE pulpitis?

Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: A lingering response after removal of the stimulus indicates irreversible inflammation of the pulp.

Subject: Endodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6017): The treatment of choice for internal (inflammatory) root resorption in a restorable permanent tooth is:

Detailed: The resorptive defect is disinfected and filled, often with thermoplasticized gutta-percha or MTA to adapt to the irregular cavity. Untreated lesions can perforate the root, worsening the prognosis.
Subject: Endodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6018): A Cvek (partial) pulpotomy is indicated for:

Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: A traumatic pulp exposure in a vital young permanent incisor

Detailed: The wound is capped with calcium hydroxide or a calcium silicate cement and sealed. Success rates exceed 90%, allowing continued root development (apexogenesis).
Subject: Endodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6019): The most common cause of inter-appointment flare-up during root canal treatment is:

Subject: Endodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6020): Which post-space preparation error most predisposes an endodontically treated tooth to root fracture?

Detailed: At least 1 mm of circumferential dentin should remain, 4-5 mm of apical gutta-percha must be preserved for the seal, and the post should fit passively; rigid oversized posts act as wedges under load.
Subject: Endodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6021): The width of the attached gingiva is calculated clinically by:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6022): In the Glickman classification, a Grade II furcation involvement is best described as:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6023): The gold-standard soft tissue graft for predictable root coverage of Miller Class I recession is:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6024): The recommended probing force for periodontal examination is approximately:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: A light, standardized force of about 0.25 N detects the pocket base without penetrating inflamed connective tissue excessively.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6025): Occlusal trauma in the absence of plaque-induced inflammation produces which change?

Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Trauma from occlusion alone causes adaptive PDL widening and mobility but never initiates pockets or attachment loss.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6026): Splinting of periodontally involved teeth is primarily indicated when:

Subject: Periodontic

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6027): Why is bleeding on probing often REDUCED in smokers despite active periodontitis?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6029): The primary objective of the modified Widman flap is to:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6030): Which systemic antibiotic combination is the classic adjunct for the molar-incisor pattern (formerly aggressive) periodontitis?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6031): Alveolar osteitis (dry socket) typically presents:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6034): During extraction of a maxillary molar, a large maxillary tuberosity fractures but remains attached to periosteum. The best management is to:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6035): Gustatory sweating of the cheek after parotid surgery (Frey syndrome) results from:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6132): The highest risk of medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw is associated with:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6133): The FIRST measure for a patient who returns with a bleeding socket several hours after extraction is:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6141): The classic triad of Behçet disease is:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6142): Regarding malignant potential, oral lichen planus:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6143): In the Newton classification of denture stomatitis, Type II represents:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6144): Burning mouth syndrome (primary type) is diagnosed when:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6145): The biopsy used to support a diagnosis of Sjögren syndrome samples:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6146): After primary infection, herpes simplex virus type 1 establishes latency in the:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6149): A dentigerous cyst characteristically attaches to the involved tooth at the:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6151): Radiographically, cemento-ossifying fibroma differs from fibrous dysplasia in that ossifying fibroma:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6152): The peripheral giant cell granuloma is distinctive among gingival nodules because it:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6153): Verrucous carcinoma differs from conventional squamous cell carcinoma in that it:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6155): A soft, yellowish, freely movable submucosal nodule of the buccal mucosa that seems to "slip" under the palpating finger is most likely a:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6157): Idiopathic osteosclerosis (dense bone island) is distinguished from condensing osteitis because idiopathic osteosclerosis:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6161): Correct infection control for an intraoral digital sensor is:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6162): On periapical films, the mandibular canal appears as:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6167): Compared with permanent teeth, primary teeth have:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6173): The Hall technique for carious primary molars involves:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6269): Taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by:

Detailed: The posterior third (taste and sensation) belongs to the glossopharyngeal nerve - which is also the afferent limb of the gag reflex.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6270): The afferent (sensory) limb of the gag reflex is mediated by which cranial nerve?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Touching the posterior pharynx stimulates glossopharyngeal afferents; the motor response travels via the vagus - the IX-in, X-out arc.
Detailed: Topical anesthesia of the posterior tongue/pharynx exploits this pathway to suppress gagging during impressions and radiographs.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6271): All motor innervation of the tongue musculature (except palatoglossus) is supplied by:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: The hypoglossal nerve drives all intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles except palatoglossus (vagus/pharyngeal plexus).
Detailed: Testing: protrusion deviates TOWARD the side of a hypoglossal lesion - relevant after surgery or in medical screening.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6272): The parotid (Stensen) duct opens into the oral cavity:
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: In the floor of the mouth beside the frenum
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 4: On the buccal mucosa opposite the maxillary second molar
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: On the buccal mucosa opposite the maxillary second molar
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Stensen's duct pierces the buccinator and opens at a papilla opposite the maxillary second molar - the landmark for inspection, milking and cannulation.
Detailed: The submandibular (Wharton) duct opens at the sublingual caruncle beside the lingual frenum - its long upward course explains its stone predilection.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6273): For an inferior alveolar nerve block, the needle is deposited within which anatomical space?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: The IAN block targets the pterygomandibular space - bounded by the medial ramus laterally and medial pterygoid muscle medially - where the nerve descends toward the mandibular foramen.
Detailed: The lingual nerve lies anteromedial in the same space (anesthetized en route); a needle too deep and posterior can enter the parotid and paralyze the facial nerve transiently.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6274): An infection of the maxillary canine region can spread to the cavernous sinus via which valveless route?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: The canine space drains through the angular vein to the ophthalmic veins, which are valveless and communicate directly with the cavernous sinus.
Detailed: Cavernous sinus thrombosis presents with proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, chemosis and fever - a life-threatening complication demanding aggressive antibiotics and drainage.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6275): In a complete upper-airway obstruction that cannot be relieved, an emergency surgical airway is established through the:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Cricothyrotomy pierces the subcutaneous cricothyroid membrane between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages - the fastest, safest emergency airway site.
Detailed: Formal tracheostomy is an operating-room procedure through lower tracheal rings; it is not an emergency chairside technique.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6276): In the FDI two-digit system, the quadrants of the PRIMARY dentition are numbered:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Primary quadrants run 5 (upper right) to 8 (lower right); thus tooth 85 is the lower-right second primary molar.
Detailed: Permanent quadrants are 1-4. The Universal system instead letters primary teeth A-T, a frequent source of chart confusion between systems.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6277): The cusp of Carabelli, when present, is located on which surface?

Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: Buccal of the mandibular first molar

Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: This accessory fifth cusp sits on the mesiolingual (mesiopalatal) cusp of the permanent maxillary first molar - and often on the second primary maxillary molar.
Detailed: It is a heritable trait, most prevalent in European populations, and its groove is a caries-susceptible site worth sealing.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6278): Which tooth has the longest average root length in the permanent dentition?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: The maxillary canine's root averages about 17 mm - the longest in the dentition - anchoring the corner of the arch.
Detailed: That length underlies the canine's longevity, its role as the ideal overdenture and clasp abutment, and the "canine eminence" of the alveolus.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6279): Physiologic secondary dentin differs from tertiary dentin in that secondary dentin:
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 3: Forms slowly throughout life after root completion, on the entire pulpal surface
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Forms slowly throughout life after root completion, on the entire pulpal surface
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Secondary dentin is the slow, age-related deposition over the whole pulp chamber (fastest on the roof and floor), while tertiary dentin forms focally in response to an irritant.
Detailed: Tertiary dentin subdivides into reactionary (by original odontoblasts) and reparative (by newly differentiated odontoblast-like cells) - the distinction depends on injury severity.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6280): Odontoblast cell bodies are located in the pulp periphery, while their processes extend:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Each odontoblast leaves a cytoplasmic process inside its dentinal tubule; the cell bodies line the pulp - dentin is therefore a vital, innervated-by-proxy tissue.
Detailed: Fluid movement within these tubules stimulating pulpal A-delta fibers (the hydrodynamic mechanism) underlies dentin sensitivity.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6281): Cementum is normally thickest at which location?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: The root apex and interradicular areas
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 4: It is uniform along the root
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: The root apex and interradicular areas
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Cementum thickness increases apically - from ~20-50 um cervically to 150-200 um or more at the apex - and continues to be deposited through life.
Detailed: Apical deposition compensates for occlusal wear and eruption; excessive deposition is hypercementosis. Cellular cementum dominates apically, acellular cervically.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6282): The average width of the healthy periodontal ligament space is approximately:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: The PDL averages about 0.25 mm (range ~0.15-0.38 mm), narrowest at the mid-root fulcrum and wider at the crest and apex.
Detailed: Uniform radiographic widening suggests occlusal trauma or scleroderma; localized widening raises suspicion of vertical fracture or, when irregular, malignancy.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6283): Under unstimulated (resting) conditions, the largest contribution to whole saliva comes from which gland?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: At rest the submandibular glands supply about two-thirds of saliva; with stimulation the serous parotid takes over as the major contributor (~50%+).
Detailed: Total daily flow is roughly 0.5-1.5 L. Unstimulated flow below 0.1 mL/min defines hyposalivation, the objective basis of xerostomia workup.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6284): The principal buffering system of stimulated saliva is:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Bicarbonate concentration rises steeply with flow rate and provides most of stimulated saliva's buffering, neutralizing plaque acids after meals.
Detailed: This is the rationale for sugar-free chewing gum after eating; at low flow the weaker phosphate and protein systems dominate, one reason xerostomic patients decay rapidly.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6285): Chewing sugar-free gum reduces caries risk primarily by:
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Stimulating salivary flow, clearance and bicarbonate buffering
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Stimulating salivary flow, clearance and bicarbonate buffering
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Gum-stimulated saliva accelerates sugar clearance, buffers plaque pH and delivers minerals for remineralization - the proven anticaries mechanism.
Detailed: Xylitol-sweetened gum adds a modest specific effect: S. mutans takes up xylitol into a futile metabolic cycle, reducing counts with habitual use.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6286): Which salivary protein family supersaturates saliva with calcium phosphate yet prevents spontaneous precipitation onto teeth?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Statherin and acidic proline-rich proteins inhibit crystal growth while keeping saliva supersaturated - enamel is bathed in a remineralizing but non-calcifying fluid.
Detailed: The same proteins form the acquired pellicle within minutes of cleaning; pellicle protects enamel but is also the substrate for bacterial adhesion.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6287): The tooth most commonly congenitally missing of ALL teeth (including third molars) is the:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Third molars are absent in roughly 20% of people - by far the most frequent agenesis; among the remaining teeth the mandibular second premolar leads.
Detailed: Hypodontia patterns are heritable (MSX1, PAX9 mutations in familial forms); multiple missing teeth warrant syndrome consideration (e.g., ectodermal dysplasia).
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6288): Which permanent teeth most frequently exhibit dens invaginatus (dens in dente)?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: The maxillary lateral incisor is the classic site of dens invaginatus - an enamel-lined infolding of the crown that may communicate with the pulp.
Detailed: Deep invaginations decay early and can cause pulp necrosis in an apparently intact tooth; prophylactic sealing of the pit is recommended at eruption.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6289): Talon cusp is an accessory cusp arising from which surface?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: A talon cusp projects from the cingulum of an incisor (usually maxillary) toward the incisal edge, often containing a pulp horn.
Detailed: Reduction must therefore be gradual with fluoride/desensitization or accompanied by pulp management; it may interfere with occlusion and esthetics.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6290): Gemination differs from fusion in that a geminated tooth typically shows:
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: One fewer tooth in the arch count
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: A normal tooth count when the anomalous crown is counted as one
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 3: Two separate root canal systems always

Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Gemination is one tooth germ incompletely dividing - a bifid crown on one root/canal with a NORMAL count; fusion joins two germs, usually reducing the count by one.
Detailed: Counting teeth is the classic exam discriminator, though fusion with a supernumerary can mimic gemination; management is esthetic recontouring or complex restoration.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6291): Enamel pearls, which can hinder scaling and contribute to localized periodontal destruction, occur most commonly at:
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 3: The furcation areas of maxillary molars
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: The furcation areas of maxillary molars
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: These ectopic enamel droplets form near furcations of maxillary (then mandibular) molars, preventing connective tissue attachment where they sit.
Detailed: They appear radiographically as small smooth radiopacities at the furcation; cervical enamel projections are the related, more common furcation-invasion risk factor.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6292): Which cells of the oral epithelium are the antigen-presenting "sentinels"?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Dendritic Langerhans cells in the suprabasal epithelium capture antigens and present them to T lymphocytes - central to contact allergy and lichenoid reactions.
Detailed: Merkel cells are touch receptors and melanocytes produce pigment; all three are non-keratinocyte residents of the epithelium.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6293): The oral mucosa lining the hard palate and gingiva is classified as:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Masticatory mucosa - keratinized stratified squamous epithelium tightly bound to bone (mucoperiosteum) - covers the hard palate and gingiva to bear frictional load.
Detailed: Lining mucosa (cheeks, floor, soft palate) is nonkeratinized and mobile; specialized mucosa of the tongue dorsum bears papillae and taste buds. The distinction predicts ulcer behavior and graft choices.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6294): Which fluoride concentration defines the standard "high-fluoride" prescription toothpaste for high-caries-risk adults?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Prescription 1.1% NaF toothpaste provides 5000 ppm fluoride - indicated for root-caries risk, xerostomia and rampant caries in patients over ~16 years.
Detailed: Regular pastes contain 1000-1500 ppm. The 12300 ppm figure is professionally applied APF gel territory, not a home toothpaste.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6295): The predominant anticaries mechanism of fluoride is:
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Systemic incorporation into enamel before eruption
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 3: Topical enhancement of remineralization and inhibition of demineralization at the plaque-enamel interface
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Topical enhancement of remineralization and inhibition of demineralization at the plaque-enamel interface
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Fluoride works chiefly post-eruptively and topically: low ambient levels drive fluorapatite-like remineralization and slow acid dissolution.
Detailed: This modern understanding (Featherstone, ten Cate) shifted emphasis from supplements toward frequent low-dose topical exposure - fluoridated water plus twice-daily paste.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6296): Dental plaque resists rinsing and mouthwash penetration primarily because it is:
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: A random pile of food debris
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 4: A structured biofilm with an extracellular polysaccharide matrix
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: A structured biofilm with an extracellular polysaccharide matrix
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Plaque is a true biofilm: organized microcolonies in a glucan-rich matrix with fluid channels, expressing phenotypes far more resistant than planktonic bacteria.
Detailed: This is why mechanical disruption (brushing, interdental cleaning, debridement) remains irreplaceable and chemical agents are only adjuncts.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6297): In the "ecological plaque hypothesis," caries results from:
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: An environmental shift (frequent sugar, low pH) selecting aciduric bacteria within the resident flora
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: Infection by a single exogenous pathogen
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: An environmental shift (frequent sugar, low pH) selecting aciduric bacteria within the resident flora
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Repeated sugar exposure lowers plaque pH, enriching acidogenic-aciduric species (mutans streptococci, lactobacilli) at the expense of health-associated flora - disease follows the ecological shift.
Detailed: Therapeutic corollary: change the environment (diet, fluoride, flow) rather than only chasing organisms - the basis of modern caries management by risk assessment.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6298): Which micro-organism group is chiefly associated with the PROGRESSION of established dentinal caries rather than its initiation?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Lactobacilli, scarce on intact surfaces, flourish in retentive carious dentin and drive lesion progression; mutans streptococci dominate initiation on smooth surfaces.
Detailed: Salivary lactobacillus counts have long served as a dietary-carbohydrate/caries-activity marker in risk assessment.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6299): A removable acrylic appliance should be stored, when out of the mouth, in:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Acrylic resin distorts as it dries and warps in hot water; storage is in room-temperature water, never boiling, never dry.
Detailed: Daily mechanical cleaning plus soaking cleansers is advised; hypochlorite-based soaks are avoided for metal-containing appliances because of corrosion.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6300): The single most accurate intraoral site for measuring core body temperature trends chairside is sublingual placement because:
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: It is closest to the skin
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: It is the coldest area of the mouth

Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: The sublingual pocket overlies the sublingual/lingual vessels, tracking core arterial temperature within ~0.3-0.5°C - adequate for clinical screening.
Detailed: Recent hot/cold drinks and mouth breathing skew readings; fever >38°C with an odontogenic infection signals systemic involvement and escalated care.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6301): Normal adult resting pulse rate used as the baseline in dental risk assessment is:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Sixty to one hundred beats per minute is the accepted adult range; persistent rates outside it (or marked irregularity) warrant evaluation before elective care.
Detailed: Anxiety commonly elevates chairside readings - repeat after rapport; an irregularly irregular pulse suggests atrial fibrillation and medication review.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6302): According to current hypertension guidance adopted in dental settings, elective treatment is generally deferred and physician referral made when blood pressure reaches:
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: A sustained reading of about 180/110 mmHg or higher
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: A sustained reading of about 180/110 mmHg or higher
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Asymptomatic readings >=180/110 (hypertensive urgency territory) contraindicate elective care until controlled; lower stage-1/2 readings allow treatment with monitoring and referral.
Detailed: Stress-reduction protocol, effective anesthesia, and epinephrine limitation are the practical adjustments for the controlled hypertensive patient.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6303): In the ASA physical status classification, a patient with severe systemic disease that limits activity but is not incapacitating is:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: ASA III denotes severe systemic disease with functional limitation - e.g., stable angina on exertion, poorly controlled diabetes - prompting treatment modification.
Detailed: ASA I is healthy, II mild disease without limitation, IV incapacitating disease that is a constant threat to life; the scale anchors dental risk assessment.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6304): The safest position for managing most sudden loss of consciousness in the dental chair is:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Supine positioning with feet raised restores cerebral perfusion - the definitive maneuver for vasovagal syncope, the most common office emergency.
Detailed: Exceptions: late-pregnancy patients are tilted to the left to relieve caval compression, and patients in respiratory distress prefer sitting upright.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6305): For latex-allergic patients, the operatory schedule and setup should include:
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: First appointment of the day with nitrile/vinyl gloves and latex-free armamentarium
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 3: Antihistamine premedication with normal latex use
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: First appointment of the day with nitrile/vinyl gloves and latex-free armamentarium
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Scheduling first thing minimizes airborne latex aeroallergen from the day's glove use; every item (gloves, dam, prophy cups, carpule plungers historically) must be latex-free.
Detailed: High-risk groups include spina bifida patients and healthcare workers; latex-fruit cross-reactivity (banana, avocado, kiwi, chestnut) is a useful screening clue.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6306): Nitrous oxide-oxygen sedation is absolutely contraindicated in a patient with:
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: A recent pneumothorax or vitreoretinal gas surgery
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: A recent pneumothorax or vitreoretinal gas surgery
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: N2O diffuses into closed gas spaces faster than nitrogen escapes, expanding a pneumothorax, intraocular gas bubble or obstructed middle ear - absolute contraindications.
Detailed: Relative cautions: first trimester, severe COPD, nasal obstruction, and B12-related neuropathy with chronic abuse. The fail-safe minimum is 30% oxygen delivery.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6307): Chronic occupational exposure to poorly scavenged nitrous oxide is linked to:
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 3: Inactivation of vitamin B12 with neurologic and hematologic effects
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Inactivation of vitamin B12 with neurologic and hematologic effects
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: N2O oxidizes the cobalt of vitamin B12, inhibiting methionine synthase; chronic exposure risks megaloblastic changes and neuropathy - the basis of scavenging requirements.
Detailed: Modern scavenging systems, mask fit and ventilation keep trace levels below recommended limits; reproductive effects were reported in unscavenged historical settings.
Subject: General Dentistry

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6308): A lichenoid reaction confined to mucosa in direct contact with a large old restoration is most commonly triggered by:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Contact lichenoid lesions arise on mucosa touching corroding amalgam; unlike idiopathic lichen planus they are asymmetric, localized and resolve after replacing the restoration.
Detailed: Patch testing to mercurials supports the diagnosis; drug-induced lichenoid reactions (antihypertensives, antimalarials, NSAIDs) are the systemic counterpart.
Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6309): Which oral lichen planus subtype carries the highest symptomatic burden and warrants closest surveillance?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Erosive/atrophic LP is painful, interferes with eating, requires topical steroid therapy, and shows the highest reported rates of malignant transformation among subtypes.
Detailed: Overall transformation risk of oral LP is about 1%; surveillance every 6-12 months with biopsy of changing areas is standard advice.
Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6310): First-line therapy for symptomatic erosive oral lichen planus is:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: High-potency topical steroids (e.g., clobetasol or fluocinonide in adhesive vehicle, or dexamethasone rinses) are the established first-line treatment.
Detailed: Adjuncts: antifungal cover for secondary candidiasis, topical calcineurin inhibitors for refractory cases, and short systemic steroid bursts for severe flares.
Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6311): In pemphigus vulgaris, autoantibodies are directed against:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: IgG against desmoglein 3 (with Dsg1 in mucocutaneous disease) destroys desmosomal adhesion, producing suprabasal acantholysis and flaccid blisters.
Detailed: Oral lesions are the FIRST sign in about half of cases and the site in nearly all; untreated disease was historically fatal - systemic steroids and rituximab transformed prognosis.
Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6312): A positive Nikolsky sign refers to:
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 4: Formation/extension of a blister when apparently normal skin or mucosa is rubbed
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Formation/extension of a blister when apparently normal skin or mucosa is rubbed
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Lateral pressure inducing epithelial separation - a bulla on rubbed normal tissue - indicates a fragile intraepithelial or junctional split, classically pemphigus vulgaris.
Detailed: It also occurs in pemphigoid, epidermolysis bullosa and toxic epidermal necrolysis; it is a chairside clue, not a substitute for biopsy with immunofluorescence.
Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6313): Direct immunofluorescence in mucous membrane pemphigoid characteristically shows:

Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: MMP autoantibodies target hemidesmosomal antigens (BP180, laminin-332), giving a linear band of IgG/C3 at the basement membrane and a subepithelial split.
Detailed: Pemphigus shows intercellular fishnet deposition instead. Perilesional tissue is submitted fresh (Michel medium) for DIF - formalin destroys the signal.
Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6314): The most feared complication of mucous membrane pemphigoid involves which site?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 2: Eyes - conjunctival scarring (symblepharon) leading to blindness
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Eyes - conjunctival scarring (symblepharon) leading to blindness
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Ocular MMP causes progressive conjunctival fibrosis, symblepharon formation, entropion and corneal damage; every MMP patient needs ophthalmologic evaluation.
Detailed: Oral disease commonly presents as desquamative gingivitis - a presentation shared with lichen planus and pemphigus, resolved by biopsy with DIF.
Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6315): Recurrent erythema multiforme is most often precipitated by:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: HSV is the leading trigger of recurrent EM; lesions follow the herpetic episode by days, with target skin lesions and crusted hemorrhagic lips.
Detailed: Frequent recurrences respond to suppressive antiviral therapy (acyclovir/valacyclovir). Drug-triggered severe forms belong to the SJS/TEN spectrum, now classified separately.
Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6316): Which clinical feature best distinguishes erythema multiforme from primary herpetic gingivostomatitis?
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 4: Sparing of the gingiva and typical target lesions on the skin in EM
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Sparing of the gingiva and typical target lesions on the skin in EM
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: EM produces widespread irregular oral erosions with hemorrhagic lip crusting but typically SPARES the gingiva and shows acral target lesions; primary HSV features fiery generalized gingivitis and vesicles.
Detailed: The distinction changes therapy: EM is managed with supportive care ± steroids and trigger control; primary HSV with supportive care ± early acyclovir.
Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6317): Major aphthous ulcers differ from minor aphthae principally in that major lesions:
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Exceed about 1 cm, last weeks to months, and heal WITH scarring
Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Exceed about 1 cm, last weeks to months, and heal WITH scarring
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Major (Sutton) aphthae are >1 cm, deep, may persist 6+ weeks, and scar on healing; minors are <1 cm and heal in 7-14 days without scarring.
Detailed: Herpetiform aphthae - dozens of pinpoint ulcers coalescing - are the third pattern; despite the name they are unrelated to herpesvirus.
Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6318): Recurrent oral and genital ulcers with eye inflammation and skin pathergy suggest which disease?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6319): Recurrent aphthous-like ulceration prompting hematologic screening is most importantly associated with deficiency of:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Hematinic deficiencies (iron, folate, B12) are found in up to 20% of RAS patients and correction can abolish recurrences - screening is part of the workup for atypical or adult-onset disease.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6320): Herpangina, presenting as vesicles and ulcers confined to the soft palate and fauces in a febrile child, is caused by:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6321): Koplik spots - clustered white specks on an erythematous buccal mucosa - are the pathognomonic oral prodrome of:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Koplik spots ("grains of salt on a red background") opposite the molars precede the measles skin rash by 1-2 days and are diagnostic.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6322): Bilateral fissuring at the corners of the mouth in a denture wearer is typically a mixed infection of:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6323): A chronic asymptomatic red rhomboid patch in the posterior midline of the tongue dorsum, devoid of papillae, is:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6324): Kaposi sarcoma of the palate in an HIV-positive patient is driven by which virus?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: HHV-8 (KS-associated herpesvirus) causes Kaposi sarcoma - red-purple macules progressing to nodules, with the hard palate and gingiva the classic oral sites.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6325): A distinctive fiery red band along the gingival margin in an HIV-positive patient, disproportionate to plaque and unresponsive to cleaning, is:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Linear gingival erythema is an HIV-associated candidal gingival infection: a 2-3 mm red marginal band that does not resolve with conventional plaque control.

Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6326): Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome comprises recurrent orofacial swelling, relapsing facial paralysis and:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: The classic triad is orofacial granulomatous swelling (cheilitis granulomatosa), recurrent facial nerve palsy and fissured (plicated) tongue.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6327): Black hairy tongue represents:

Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Elongation and defective desquamation of filiform papillae with pigment-producing bacteria

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6328): A solitary, small, uniformly brown macule on the lower lip of a young adult, stable for years, is most likely:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: The labial melanotic macule is a benign focal increase in melanin - small, flat, well-demarcated and unchanging, most common on the lower lip vermilion.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6329): A blue-gray macule adjacent to a large restoration, showing fine radiopaque particles on radiograph, is:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Implanted amalgam particles tattoo the mucosa gray-blue; when radiographs demonstrate metallic flecks the diagnosis is confirmed without biopsy.

Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6330): Diffuse brown mucosal pigmentation appearing with fatigue, weight loss and skin bronzing suggests:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: In Addison disease, high ACTH stimulates melanocytes: new-onset diffuse oral pigmentation may precede the cutaneous bronzing - an endocrine emergency to recognize.

Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6331): Atrophic glossitis - a smooth, red, depapillated and often burning tongue - classically reflects deficiency of:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Deficiencies of B12, folate or iron atrophy the lingual papillae, producing the smooth "beefy" or pale tongue with burning; it may precede anemia on blood counts.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6332): Plummer-Vinson (Paterson-Kelly) syndrome combines iron-deficiency anemia and esophageal webs with an elevated risk of:

Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6333): Diffuse boggy gingival enlargement with spontaneous bleeding, pallor and fatigue in an adult should raise first suspicion of:

Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Leukemic infiltration produces rapidly developing, boggy, hemorrhagic gingival enlargement; acute monocytic/myelomonocytic leukemias are most notorious.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6334): Spontaneous gingival bleeding and palatal petechiae typically appear when the platelet count falls below approximately:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Spontaneous mucosal bleeding is expected below ~20-30 x10^9/L; surgical hemostasis becomes unreliable below ~50 x10^9/L, guiding transfusion planning.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6335): Hemophilia A is a deficiency of which clotting factor, and which screening test does it prolong?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6336): The most common inherited bleeding disorder, often revealed by prolonged oozing after dental extraction, is:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Von Willebrand disease affects up to ~1% of the population; deficient vWF impairs platelet adhesion and stabilizes less factor VIII, causing mucocutaneous bleeding.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6337): For a patient with poorly controlled hyperthyroidism, epinephrine-containing anesthetics are limited or avoided because of the risk of:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: The thyrotoxic patient is catecholamine-sensitized: added epinephrine can trigger dangerous tachycardia, arrhythmia or thyroid storm - elective care waits for control.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6338): Congenital hypothyroidism (and severe juvenile hypothyroidism) characteristically shows which orofacial features?

Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Delayed tooth eruption, macroglossia and retained primary teeth
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Thyroid hormone deficiency delays growth and dental eruption; macroglossia, thick lips, and prolonged retention of primary teeth are classic.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6339): Progressive mandibular growth with recurrence of spacing between teeth in an adult, plus enlarging hands and coarse features, indicates:

Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Adult-onset GH excess reactivates condylar growth: Class III drift, new diastemas, macroglossia and enlarged hands/feet - the dentist may be first to notice.

Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6340): In chronic kidney disease, dental prescribing must particularly avoid or adjust:

Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: NSAIDs (nephrotoxic) and renally cleared drugs without dose adjustment
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: NSAIDs reduce renal perfusion and are avoided in significant CKD; renally excreted antibiotics (amoxicillin at high doses, etc.) need interval adjustment to GFR.

Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6341): A patient with advanced cirrhosis bleeds excessively after minor oral surgery primarily because of:
Ø®ÙØ§Ø± 1: Reduced hepatic synthesis of clotting factors plus thrombocytopenia of hypersplenism

Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: The failing liver synthesizes less of nearly all coagulation factors while portal hypertension sequesters platelets - INR and platelet count are checked before surgery.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6342): The safest period of pregnancy for routine dental treatment is:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Organogenesis is complete and the uterus not yet cumbersome: the second trimester (weeks 14-27) is the preferred window for elective routine care.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6343): Which analgesic is preferred throughout pregnancy for dental pain?
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Paracetamol is the analgesic of choice in pregnancy; NSAIDs are specifically avoided in the third trimester (premature ductus arteriosus closure, labor effects).

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6344): Trigeminal neuralgia in a patient under 40, bilateral, or with sensory deficit should prompt:

Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Young-onset, bilateral or atypical trigeminal neuralgia is "secondary TN" until proven otherwise - MS plaques or cerebellopontine-angle tumors must be excluded by MRI.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6345): Pain persisting more than 3 months in the distribution of a healed shingles rash is termed:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Postherpetic neuralgia - burning, allodynic pain outlasting the rash by 3+ months - is the major zoster complication, increasing sharply with age.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6346): Severe paroxysmal throat and ear pain triggered by swallowing or coughing characterizes:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Glossopharyngeal neuralgia produces shock-like pain in the tonsillar fossa, tongue base and ear, fired by swallowing, yawning or coughing.

Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6347): Strictly unilateral orbital-temporal pain attacks lasting 15-180 minutes with ipsilateral tearing, nasal congestion and restlessness define:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Cluster headache: excruciating unilateral attacks with prominent autonomic signs and motor restlessness, often nocturnal, clustering over weeks - frequently mistaken for dental pain.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6348): New temporal headache with jaw claudication and a tender, thickened temporal artery in a patient over 60 requires urgent:

Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: ESR/CRP testing and high-dose steroids to prevent blindness

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6349): Persistent idiopathic facial pain (atypical facial pain) is best characterized as:

Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: PIFP is a chronic, deep, poorly localized ache that crosses anatomical boundaries, has normal investigations, and frequently coexists with anxiety/depression.

Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6350): Persistent pain in a tooth or extraction site with entirely normal clinical and radiographic findings, often following endodontics, is best labeled:

Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6351): Primary Sjögren syndrome carries a substantially increased lifetime risk (about 5-10%) of developing:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Chronic lymphocytic stimulation in Sjögren syndrome predisposes to marginal-zone MALT lymphoma; persistent parotid enlargement, new lymphadenopathy or low C4 warrant investigation.

Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6352): Bilateral, soft, painless, slowly developing parotid enlargement in a patient with alcoholism or diabetes, with normal salivary function tests, is most consistent with:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Sialosis is a non-inflammatory, non-neoplastic acinar hypertrophy linked to alcoholism, diabetes, malnutrition and bulimia - bilateral, soft and painless.

Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6353): Acute painful bilateral parotid swelling with trismus and fever in an unvaccinated adolescent, lifting the ear lobe outward, suggests:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Mumps causes viral parotitis - bilateral in most cases, tender, with malaise and fever; the everted ear lobe is the classic sign, and the papilla shows clear (non-purulent) saliva.
Detailed: Complications rise after puberty: orchitis, oophoritis, meningitis, deafness. Diagnosis is clinical/serologic; treatment supportive.

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6354): A rapidly appearing crateriform ulcer of the posterior hard palate in a smoker, with lobular necrosis of salivary glands but preserved lobular architecture on biopsy, is:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6355): The dominant source of intrinsic halitosis in otherwise healthy patients is:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6356): A persistent metallic or altered taste (dysgeusia) is a recognized side effect of which frequently prescribed drug?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6357): Unilateral vesicles and ulcers strictly limited to one side of the palate, stopping sharply at the midline, in an older or immunosuppressed patient indicate:

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6358): The painless, indurated, clean-based ulcer of primary syphilis (chancre) at the lip or tongue appears how long after inoculation, and how does it behave?

Detailed: Serology may still be negative early; dark-field microscopy or PCR of the lesion confirms. Untreated disease proceeds to the secondary stage.
Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6359): The most characteristic oral lesions of SECONDARY syphilis are:

Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Mucous patches and split papules, highly infectious grayish erosions

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6360): A chronic, undermined, painful ulcer of the tongue dorsum in a patient with cough, night sweats and weight loss is classic for:

Ø§ÙØ¥Ø¬Ø§Ø¨Ø©: Secondary (oral) tuberculosis seeded from pulmonary disease

Detailed: Biopsy shows caseating granulomas with acid-fast bacilli; management is referral for full anti-tubercular therapy, and staff exposure review.
Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6361): A chronic suppurative jaw infection draining through skin sinuses that discharge yellow "sulfur granules" is:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Actinomyces israelii, a gram-positive filamentous commensal, invades after mucosal breach (extraction, trauma) causing woody induration and sinus tracts with characteristic granules.
Detailed: Treatment is prolonged high-dose penicillin (weeks to months) plus drainage/debridement - short courses reliably relapse.
Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6362): A chronic indurated oral ulcer in a patient from an endemic area with disseminated fungal disease and bird/bat-dropping exposure suggests:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Disseminated histoplasmosis frequently ulcerates the oral mucosa - chronic, indurated lesions mimicking carcinoma - especially in immunosuppressed patients.
Detailed: Diagnosis: biopsy with fungal stains and culture/antigen testing; treatment with itraconazole or amphotericin B for severe disease.
Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6363): Sudden swelling of the lips, tongue or floor of mouth in a patient recently started on which drug class demands airway vigilance?

Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6364): Severe persistent oral ulceration in a patient on low-dose weekly methotrexate may signal toxicity, which is prevented or treated with:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Methotrexate blocks dihydrofolate reductase; mucositis is an early toxicity sign, mitigated by routine folic acid and treated with folinic acid rescue in overdose.

Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6365): Progressive limited mouth opening with hard, board-like buccal mucosa and blanched fibrotic bands in a betel-quid/areca-nut chewer indicates:
Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Areca-nut arecoline drives juxta-epithelial fibrosis: burning with spicy food, marble-like mucosa, fibrous bands and inexorable trismus - and a malignant transformation risk of several percent.

Subject: Oral Medicine

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6366): Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) shows which characteristic orofacial combination?

Q(1): Ø§ÙØ³Ø¤Ø§Ù: Q(6367): Pyostomatitis vegetans - yellow "snail-track" pustules on erythematous oral mucosa - is a highly specific oral marker of:

Ø§ÙØªÙØ³ÙØ±: Pyostomatitis vegetans parallels bowel disease activity, most strongly ulcerative colitis; eosinophilia is common and lesions improve with control of the colitis.
